EARLY PALAEOZOIC PALAEOMAGNETISM IN AUSTRALIA
I. Cambrian results from the Flinders Ranges, South Australia
II. Late Early Cambrian results from Kangaroo Island, South Australia
III. Middle to early-Late Cambrian results from the Amadeus Basin,
Northern Territory
C.T. KLOOTWIJK
Research School of Earth Sciences, Australian National University, P.O. Box 4,
Canberra, A.C. T. 2600 (Australia)
(Received September 27,1978; accepted February 27, 1979)
ABSTRACT
Klootwijk, C.T., 1980. Early Palaeozoic palaeomagnetism in Australia. Tectonophysics,
64: 249-332.
I. Cambrian results from the Flinders Ranges, South Australia
A total of 460 samples from six sequences spanning the Cambrian succession of the
Flinders Ranges (Adelaide “Geosyncline”, South Australia) has been analyzed through
thermal demagnetization studies. All samples showed a recent field component, generally
constituting more than 50% of the initial intensity, which in most cases was removed by
200-400°C. Two characteristic magnetic components have been identified:
(A) A secondary magnetic component of Cambro-Ordovician age (S-pole at 75.3OE
26.0°N, crss = 7.4’, N = 5 localities) interpreted as having been induced by thermo-
chemical activity during a period of enhanced heat flux prior to the Late Cambrian-
Early Ordovician diastrophistic phases of the Delamarian Orogeny.
(B) A primary magnetic component, which indicates rapid polar motion during the
Early Cambrian and a much reduced polar motion during the Middle Cambrian.
Representative palaeomagnetic pole positions for the primary component are:
(1) Basal Hawker Group (earliest Cambrian): S-pole at 2.3’E 26.7’5, dp = 8.1°,
dm = 14.3’, N = 10 (sites).
(2) Billy Creek Formation-Wirrealpa Limestone-Aroona Creek Limestone (late
Early Cambrian to early Middle Cambrian): S-pole at 20.1’E 37.4OS, dp = 7.2’, dm =
14.4’, N =ll (sites).
(3) Basal Lake Frome Group (Middle Cambrian): S-pole at 26.1’E 29.3’5, dp = 6.6’,
dm = 13.1’, N = 10 (sites).
(4) Pantapinna Formation (late Middle Cambrian?): S-pole at 29.2’E 36.4’S, dp =
8.4O, dm = 16.7’, N = 4 (sites).
Available data suggest that deposition of the Lake Frome Group beds probably did not
continue into the Late Cambrian.
II. Late Early Cambrian results from Kangaroo Island, South Australia
A total of 108 block samples from a late Early Cambrian red-bed sequence on Kanga-
roo Island (Adelaide “Geosyncline”, South Australia) has been analysed through thermal
demagnetization studies.

### page_2
All samples contained a recent field component of considerable intensity. Two charac-
teristic magnetic components have been identified :
(A) A secondary magnetic component of Late Cambrian-Early Ordovician age (S-pole
at: 75.8’E 17.4’N, dp = 4.2’, dm = 7.9O , A’ = 54 specimens), attributed to thermo-
chemical activity predating the main folding phases of the Delamarian Orogeny.
(B) A primary magnetic component corrrsp!mding to a S-pole position at, 15.1’E
33.8’S (dp = 6.2O, dm = 12.3’, N = 16 sites)
Both the primary and the secondary magnetic component are in very good directional
agreement with the magnetization pattern from the correlated Billy Creek Formation
of the Flinders Ranges (I). Consequently, noticeably rotational movement since late-
Early Cambrian times between Kangaroo Island and the northwrstern part of the Adelaide
“Geosyncline” can be ruled out.
III. Middle to early-Late Cambrian results from the Amadeus Basin (Northern Territory)
A total of 328 samples from a Middle Cambrian red-bed succession and a Middle to
early-Late Cambrian carbonate succession in the Amadeus Basin (Central Australia)
have been analyzed through thermal demagnetization studies.
All samples contained a recent field component of considerable intensity which
became broken down, respectively below 2OO’C in the carbonate samples and between
3OO’C and 5OO’C in the red-bed samples. Another recent field component, broken down
between 600°C and 675’C, was noted in some of the red-bed samples.
Three characteristic magnetic components have been identified:
(A) A secondary magnetic component of Late Devonian-Early Carboniferous age
(S-pole at 110.5’E 46.9’S, N = 2 localities) which predates the main folding phase of the
Early Carboniferous Alice Springs Orogeny
(B) Another secondary magnetic component (S-pole at 60.8’E 33.8’N, N = 2 localities)
which is very similar to a thermo-chemically induced Cambro-Ordovician magnetic com-
ponent, noted in rocks from the Adelaide “Geosyncline”.
(C) A primary magnetic component which suggests reduced polar motion during the
Middle Cambrian (S-pole at 16.6’E 35.0°S, (~95 = 7.4’, N = 5 sites) and rapid polar
motion during the early-Late Cambrian (S-pole at 34.9OE 14.9ON, dp = 6.3’, dm = 11.6’.
N = 9 specimens).
The thermally obtained palaeomagnetic record from the red-bed sequences seems less
well suited for magnetostratigraphic purposes than that from the carbonate sequences.
The magnetic polarity record in the former has become obscured as result of a prolonged
acquisition phase. In contrast, the red-bed sequences generally showed a better concen-
tration of component directions when compared with the carbonate sequences.
Combined results from the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and the Amadeus Basin indicate the
Early and Middle Cambrian as a predominantly reversed polarity interval during which
several shorter periods of mixed polarity occurred. A succeeding normal polarity interval
started in the early-Late Cambrian and rapid polar motion took place during the Early
Cambrian and the Cambro-Ordovician, whereas the Precambrian-Cambrian boundary
period and the Middle Cambrian were quasi-static intervals.
The agreement between Middle Cambrian data from the Amadeus Basin and from the
Adelaide “Geosyncline” indicates unity of the Australian plate at least since that time.
A common apparent polar wander path for the Gondwanaland continents backwards
till at least 750 m.y. ago can be constructed through available palaeomagnetic data.
The suggested late Proterozoic part of this APW remains open to alternative interpreta-
tions.

### page_3
251
I. Cambrian results from the Flinders Ranges, South Australia
INTRODUCTION
Late Proterozoic and early Phanerozoic palaeomagnetic data from the
Gondwanaland continents were reinterpreted recently by McElhinny et al.
(19’7413) and McElhinny and Embleton (1976). Using selected pole positions,
they showed that a common apparent polar wanderpath (APW) can be
drawn when the main Gondwanaland fragments are reunited into the Smith
and Hallam (1970) reconstruction. This common APW stretches from the
ultimate Late Jurassic breakup backwards to at least 750 m.y. ago, thus
implying unity of Gondwanaland during this period. Their proposed APW
(south poles) has the shape of double question mark; one half spanning the
late Proterozoic and the other half spanning the early Phanerozoic. The overall
structure of this APW is certainly acceptable, but detailed examination
indicates several discrepancies which make their proposed APW open to
improvement and reinterpretation.
One of the major uncertainties in constructing APW’s which span periods
of appreciable polar movement is the inherent difficulty in assigning poles
to either the normal or the reversed polarity group. McElhinny et al.%
interpretation of polarities presently seems to be the more viable and less
complicated approach. However, alternative backwards continuations of the
Gondwanaland APW from its well defined late Palaeozoic trajectory, by
reversing polarity of early Phanerozoic and latest Proterozoic palaeomagnetic
poles (Piper, 1973; Schmidt and Morris, 1977) certainly cannot be ruled out.
More palaeomagnetic poles are required in the less densely populated trajec-
tories of appreciable polar wandering to solve this polarity ambiguity and for
a better definition of the Gondwanaland APW.
The late Proterozoic segment of McElhinny et al.‘s common APW is long
and is only sparsely covered with pole positions. Recently, new results from
sections in the Amadeus Basin (Central Australia) spanning the Precam-
brian-Cambrian boundary period were reported by Kirschvink (1978a, b),
and McWilliams (1977) finalized comprehensive palaeomagnetic studies on
the late Proterozoic from Australia, mainly from the Adelaide “Geosyn-
cline” and the Amadeus Basin, and from southern Africa. McWilliams’
interpretation of late Proterozoic palaeomagnetic data from Gondwanaland
differs notably from McElhinny et al’s APW, but the Cambrian data
presented in this series of papers (Sections I, II, III) show that McWilliams’
late Proterozoic results also can be interpreted in support of McElhinny et
al’s APW. (cf. Fig. 111.13).
The early Palaeozoic part of McElhinny et al.‘s common APW also appears
to be somewhat problematic. Several pole positions, especially those from
the Adelaide “Geosyncline”, are out of sequence, whilst others - notably
some South American and African data-appear to diverge from the
proposed path. Therefore, I have initiated palaeomagnetic studies on well

### page_4
252
developed early Palaeozoic sequences in Australia, namely in the Amadeus
Basin and in the Adelaide “Geosyncline”.
The recent availability of a sensitive cryogenic magnetometer facilitates
palaeomagnetic studies on weakly magnetized sedimentary rocks such as
carbonates. Such a widening spectrum of prospective lithologies and a con-
sequent better documentation of the palaeomagnetic record ultimately may
clarify the ambiguous polarity assignment of early Palaeozoic and older
rocks.
I report here new results from carbonate and red beds successions span-
ning the Cambrian sequence of the Flinders Ranges, South Australia.
GEOLOGICAL SETTING
The Adelaide “Geosyncline” in southern Australia (Fig. 1.1; Thompson
et al., 1976) represents a mainly meridionally aligned downwarped region
of complex fractured basement, with a thick intracratonic accumulation of
sedimentary rocks. Sedimentation commenced probably between 1300 and
1400 m.y. ago, although a possible much younger age limit of about 900
m.y. has been suggested by Cooper (1975) and McWilliams (1977), and con-

tinued intermittently with only minor volcanic activity until the onset of
the Cambro-Ordovician Delamarian Orogeny (Fig. 1.2).
The Adelaide “Geosyncline” is separated from the Gawler craton to the
west by a north-south trending belt of fractures, the Torrens Hinge zone.
The Adelaide “Geosyncline” is discordantly bounded to the southeast by
the Cambrian Kanmantoo trough, but the extent of the Adelaide “Geo-
syncline” to the west (Wopfner, 1966, 1970) is not very well known because
of cover rock.
During the Cambro-Ordovician Delamarian Orogeny, the contents of the
Kanmantoo trough and the Adelaide “Geosyncline” were folded, faulted
and metamorphosed. Pre- to syntectonic granite intruded the eastern part

### page_6
254
of the Delamarian fold belt (515-506 m.y., Milnes et al., 1977), followed
locallyb y post-erogenic granitic intrusion like in the Mount Painter region
(460~-430 my., Compston et al., 1966; Coats and Blissets, 1971).
Effects of regional met~orphism are confined mostly to the southern,
eastern and extreme northern areas of the orogen, with the metamorphic
grade generally decreasing in a northwesterly direction. Lower greenschist
facies metamorphism is evident in the Mount Lofty Ranges, but the central
part of the Flinders Ranges has not been visibly affected.
Northwest to northeast trending synsedimentary faults and recently
disputed diapiric st~ctures (Webb, 1961; Coats, 1965; Dalgarno and
Johnson, 1968; Burns et al., 1977) controlled thickness and facies of the
Adelaidean and Cambrian sediments. Cratonic areas to the west (Gawler
craton), north (Mount Painter block) and east (a.o. the Willyama inlier) have
acted as the major sediment sources.
The bulk of the sediments of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” is made up by
middle to late Proterozoic rocks of the Adelaide System (Fig. 1.2;
Thompson et al., 1976), which were studied palaeomagnetically by
McWilliams (1977). The present study concerns the well exposed Cambrian
sequence of the Flinders Ranges and its stratigraphy will be described
briefly (Fig. 1.2).
A distinct erosional disconformity between the Ediacara fauna bearing
Pound Quartzite, i.e. the topmost formation of the Wilpena Group (Adelaide
System), and the overlying Uratanna Formation supposedly covers the
Precambrian-Cambrian boundary (Daily, 1973, 1974). This late Adelaidean
regressive period was followed by a transgression at the onset of the Cam-
brian, associated with gradual subsidence of the basin floor of the “Geosyn-
cline” throughout Early Cambrian times. Continuing shallow water type
sedimentation, generally dark coloured carbonates and shales, indicates that
sedimentation and subsidence rates were similar. Pronounced synsedimen-
tary faulting and diapirism resulted in heterotopical facies changes in the
Lower Cambrian Hawker Group (Fig. 1.2). At the end of the Early Cam-
brian, a regression associated with the Kangarooian movements (Daily and
Forbes, 1969) led to the slightly evaporitic red-bed environment of the
Billy Creek Formation and was followed by a short lived period of wide-
spread carbonate deposition (Wirrealpa Limestone, Aroona Creek Lime-
stone) at the beginning of the Middle Cambrian. Reversion to a high energy
red-bed environment characterizes most of the Lake Frome Group sedimen-
tation. These high-energy deposits are attributed to the end phase of the
Kangarooian movements (Daily and Forbes, 1969) and herald the onset of
the Delamarian Orogeny which started during Late Cambrian times. Con-
tinuity of sedimentation above the Lake Frome Group is unknown in the
Flinders Ranges.
Trace fossils in the Uratanna and Parachilna Formations and a gastropod
fauna in the Parachilna Formation indicate an early Early Cambrian age.
Well developed faunal assemblages (Daily, 1956) in the Lower Cambrian

### page_7
255
Hawker Group, with an abundant development of Archaeocyatha (Walter,
1967), allow correlation across the many local facies developments. Rare
trilobite occurrences indicate a late-Early Cambrian age for the Billy Creek
Formation, whereas abundant faunas in the overlying Wirrealpa Limestone
and the correlated Aroona Creek Limestone indicate an early Middle Cam-
brian age. Sporadic trilobite finds in the two lowermost formations of the
Lake Frome Group, i.e. the Moodlatana Formation and the Balcoracana
Formation, indicate Middle- and late-Middle Cambrian ages, respectively.
Fossils are seemingly absent in the overlying Pantapinna Sandstone and the
Grindstone Range Sandstone, i.e. the topmost formations of the Lake Frome
Group. A Late Cambrian age, possibly reaching into the Early Ordovician
(B. Daily, in Thompson et al., 1976) has been suggested for these forma-
tions. As will be discussed later, comparison of the palaeomagnetic data
presented here with new data from the Amadeus Basin [Section III] suggests
that most, if not all, of the Lake Frome Group sedimentation was confined
to the Middle Cambrian.
SAMPLING LOCALITIES
Samples, spanning the Cambrian sedimentation record, were collected at
six localities in the central Flinders Ranges (Fig. I.lB).
(1) Parachilna Gorge (138.53”E 31.12”s)
Three sites (APRA-APRC) were taken in the more basal part of the
Parachilna Formation at Parachilna Gorge in reddish to locally discoloured
argillaceous sandstone beds with well developed vertical burrow tracks, about
9-15 m above the contact with the underlying Pound Quartzite.
(2) Bunyeroo Gorge (138.55”E 31.41”s)
The Hawker Group has been sampled in the gorge itself, and the overlying
Billy Creek Formation-Wirrealpa Limestone sequence has been sampled
along a profile to the southwest of the gorge.
Hawker Group. Eleven sites (AWIA-AWIE, APAB-APAG) have been
taken over a total stratigraphic thickness of about 500 m through massive
limestone banks of the Wilkawillina Formation, and interfingering sequences
of dark grey nodular and thinly bedded limestones and shales of the Parara
Formation. The Parara facies represents strongly reducing conditions (Daily,
1972b), which may have resulted in its poor palaeomagnetic characteristics.
Another two sites (AORA-AORB) were taken in thinly bedded green
shales in the basal part of the overlying Oraparina Formation, which is
poorly exposed at the western entrance of the gorge.
Billy Creek Formation-Wirrealpa Limestone. Three sites (ABCE-ABCG)
were taken throughout a flaggy dolomitic limestone bank about 3 m thick

### page_8
256
chosen by Dalgarno (1964) as the base of the Billy Creek Formation. Two
sites (ABCC-ABCD) were sampled about 175 m above the base of the Billy
Creek Formation in thinly bedded dark red mudstones of the basal member.
Another two sites (ABCA-ABCD) were taken at a small hillock further to
the southwest, about 100 m stratigraphically below the top of the forma-
tion, in reddish to pink coloured micaceous sandstones which form the
upper member of the formation.
Two sites {AWRA-AWRB) were taken in the Wirrealpa Limestone. Site
AWRB was taken in a massive dolomitic limestone bank at the base of the
formation, whereas site AWRA was taken in a rubbly limestone bank about
75 m higher stratigraphically.
(3) Mount Scott Area (138.35”E 30.61”s)
Ajax Limestone. Fifty-two block samples (BAJAl-52) were taken at
regular intervals of l-2 m through the top 80 m of the Ajax Limestone,
along a prominent creek south of Aroona Dam. The sequence consists of
light red to pink argillaceous limestone which becomes progressively more
massive towards the higher part of the section. The Ajax Limestone is
correlated with the carbonates of the Hawker Group in the central Flinders
Ranges (Daily,1956; B. Daily, in Thompson et al., 1976).
Aroona Creek Limestone. Another 24 block samples {BACAl-24) were
taken through the top 25 m of this formation, consisting of pale coloured
well bedded dolomitic limestone, well exposed where the formation cuts
the Aroona Creek. The basal part of the Aroona Creek Limestone has been
correlated with the Wirrealpa Limestone (Daily, 1956; Daily, in Thompson
et al., 1976) since both contain a Redlichia fauna.
(4) coast Billy Creek (138.92”E 31.27”s)
The well described Cambrian sequence of Mount Billy Creek (Daily, 1956;
Dalgarno, 1964) shows a peculiar facies development attributed to syn-
sedimentary faulting associated with the Oraparina diapir. Diapiric activity
is thought to have ended during deposition of the Wirrealpa Limestone
(Coats, 1965: Dalgarno and Johnson 1968; Youngs, 1976). Strati~aphic
profiles were sampied through the topmost beds of the Billy Creek Forma-
tion, the Wirrealpa Limestone and the Moodlatana Formation.
Silly Creek Formation. Four sites (BBCA-BBCD) were taken through
prominent sandstone banks at the top 24 m of the Billy Creek Formation.
~~rre~~~~ Limestone. Eleven sites (BWIA-BWIK) were taken over a
stratigraphic interval of 120 m in the more coherent banks of the formation,
made up of mottled limestones with some massive limestone banks at the
base.
Moodlatuna Formation. Forty seven samples (BMOOl-47) were drilled at

One site (AWRC) was taken in well bedded massive oolitic limestones, in

(6) Balcoracana Creek (138.92” E 31.15” S)
Lake Frome Group sediments are well exposed in this profile.
~oodl~tana Formation. Two sites (AMOA, AMOB) have been taken about

SAMPLING TECHNIQUE AND LABORATORY TREATMENT
Where local conditions pe~~t~d core samples were obtained with a
portable l-inch diamond drill. Otherwise block-samples were taken (Mount
Scott area), which were cored in the laboratory with a drill press. The
samples were orientated in the field with both a magnetic and a solar com-
pass using a device similar to that described by Embleton and Edwards
(1973).
Samples were taken either as separate sites generally consisting of 6-8
samples or, if conditions permitted, as stratigraphic profiles with each sample
taken from a separate bed at regular 1-2 m intervals. Stratigraphic intervals
were measured with a Jacob’s Staff and an attached Abney level. Mostly two
specimens, 2.5 cm diameter and 2.25 cm height, were sliced from each core.
Up to three specimens from each site, or one specimen from each third
sample in case of stratigraphic profiles, have been subjected to progressive
thermal demagnetization studies. The heatings were done in air in a furnace
described by McElhinny et al. (1971). Because of the complexity of magne-
tization, all pilot specimens were progressively demagnetized in 12-18 steps
with decreasing temperature intervals up to 685°C. The intensity of suscep-
tibility was measured after each heating step on a Digico bulk susceptibility
unit. The remaining specimens were subjected to partial progressive demag-

### page_10
258
netization in 8-12 steps over a selected temperature interval. Care was taken
to keep the specimens in a very much reduced magnetic environment since
the specimens tended to acquire Viscous Remanent Magnetization (VRM)
after the higher heating steps.
Two pilot specimens from each site from the Bunyeroo Gorge, Balcora-
cana Creek, Parachilna Gorge and Red Hill Well localities were subjected to
a progressive al~rnating field demagnetization in 12-20 steps up to 210 mT
in a two-axis specimens tumbler. Because of excessive development of
spurious components and failure to isolate separate components completely,
further AFdemagnetization was not pursued for the bulk of the samples.
All magnetic measurements were made on a SCT 2-axis super-conducting
rock magnetometer which was interfaced to a Digico mini-computer for
immediate data reduction.
Directional analysis of all specimen components was made by means of
orthogonal projection figures (Zijderveld, 1967, 1975).
RESULTS
A limiting factor for remanence measurement of carbonate rocks in
particular was a strong development of viscous m~etization after heating
above 400-450°C. Because of the individual behaviour of the specimens
during thermal demagnetization, laborious demagnetization series had to
be run coupled with careful analysis of the orthogonal projection figures.
Within a site and even within a sample, individual magnetic components
often showed widely different blocking temperature ranges.
Throughout this study and especially in the lower intensity carbonate
samples it was observed that the dem~etization paths often bypassed the
origin of the projection figure during breakdown of what can be interpreted
as the last remaining magnetic component. The reason for this bypassing is
not completely understood. Various possible causes may be mentioned:
(a) Inhomogeneous magnetization (Collinson, 1977), which becomes more
prominent after continued demagnetization.
(b) Presence of an unidentified additional magnetic component.
(c) Acquisition of a VRM due to a slight residual field within the super-
conducting shield. It has to be mentioned, however, that similar observations
have been made during earlier studies of carbonate samples on a Jelinek JR-3
spinner (Klootwijk and VandenBerg, 1975; VandenBerg et al., 1978) and
during red-bed measurements with an astatic magnetometer (Klootwijk,
1974). So this observation cannot be attributed solely to supposed deficien-
ces in measuring apparatus.
Clearly, orthogonal projection figures are a most useful tool for analyses
of such samples. Component directions can be determined by reading the
first derivative of straight trajectories of the vector graph, which is analogous
to a smoothed analytical vector subtraction.
In general, three magnetic components could be distinguished (Tables
1.1-1.3):

(Fig. 1.3B). This RFC was generally eliminated at the lower temperature
ranges (Table 1.4). During thermal analysis at the higher temperature ranges,
generally two characteristic magnetic components could be distinguished.
(b) A SSW-SW directed component (A) with a moderate to low upwards
dip. Both normal and reversed polarities are present.
(c) A WNW-NNW directed component (B) with a low downwards dip,

and of both normal and reversed polarity, This component was particularly
noticeable in samples from the eastern Flinders Ranges and from the Mount
Scott area, but was less prominent in samples from the western Flinders
Ranges.

main magnetic characteristics of the various formations, and also those
characteristics which need special comment are described below. Other

Paruchilna Formation (Parachilna Gorge)
A characteristic magnetic component (A) was gradually broken down
(Fig. 1.5A, B) with an evident blocking temperature range between 600°C
and 675°C (Fig, 1.6A). The susceptibility decreased noticeably at temper-
atures above 400” C.

### page_16
264

### page_17
~~~~e~ Group (Bunyeroo Gorge)
In limestone samples of the Wilkawillina facies, (sites AWIA-AWIC and
APAG) and also in site AORA of the Oraparina Shale, an A-component
(reversed polarity) was separated at temperatures between 250°C and
480°C (Figs. 1.4A, 1.5C). Excessive build-up of VRM associated with a very
rapid increase in susceptibility prevented further thermal ~eatment. A
particular difficulty with the Parara-type limestones was an interpreted
composite breakdown at constant ratio of the slight remaining RFC and the
A-component at temperatures above 250°C. This resulted in an intriguing
pattern of pseudostable directions which had to be rejected (Table 1.1).
Ajax milestone @IMount Scott area)
In the lower half of the sequence, a RFC was the only component
(Fig. 1.4, 1.5D) which could be separated up to 680°C. In addition to this
RFC, an A- and a B-component of both normal and reversed polarity were
more dom~antly present in the upper half of the section (Fig. 1.4C, 1.5E, F).
The RFC then became completely broken down between 200°C and 45O”C,
with the A- and B-components broken down separately at higher temper-
atures up to 680°C. Individuality of the specimens was very apparent and no
distinct temperature intervals could be distinguished for the A- and B-com-
ponents. In a few samples only, an A- and a B-component were simul-
taneously present, the B-component was then broken down at the lower
temperatures up to 600°C and the A-component at the higher temperatures.
Mostly, however, only either an A- or a B-component could be isolated, with
different specimens from the same sample containing different components.
All samples showed a gradual breakdown of the characteristic magnetic com-
ponent and no evident blocking range was visible {Fig. 1.6L). Susceptibility
increased very rapidly above 500°C (Fig. 1.6V), but build-up of VRM was
not so strong that it prevented further measurement, as was generally the
case with the non-reddish carbonates.

Billy Creek ~o~rn~t~on (Bunyeroo Gorge, Mount Billy Creek)
(a) Basal dolomitic limestone (Bunyeroo Gorge). An A-component of
reversed polarity was separately and gradually broken down from about
260°C till 460°C (Fig. 1,5G, H). Excessive VRM build-up and strong increase
in susceptibility became apparent only at more elevated temperatures and
did not prevent the determination of the A-component.
(b) Red-bed sequence (Bunyeroo Gorge, Mount Billy Creek). An A-com-
ponent of both normal and reversed polarity was broken down separately
above 400°C (Fig. 1.5J, K). Samples from the more sandy top member
showed two distinct blocking temperature ranges, one around 500°C and

### page_21
269
another above 600°C (Fig. 1.6F, G). Only the latter blocking temperature
range was present in the samples from the basal member with the higher
carbonate content (ABCC, ABCD, Fig. 1.6E). A notable exception were
site ABCB samples which did not show any evidence of a distinct blocking
temperature range. Therefore, these internally very consistent but aberrant
directions have been discarded.
A B-component was not identified in samples from the Bunyeroo Gorge
section but this component was present in some specimens from the Mount
Billy Creek section, and became broken down gradually between 400°C and
680°C. In case both an A- and a B-component were present in the same
specimen, the A-component then became broken down below 600°C and the
B-component above 600°C. The susceptibility of samples from the sandy top
member generally decreased above 400°C (Fig. 1.6S), whereas the samples
from the more calcareous basal member showed an increase in susceptibility
at the higher temperatures.
Wirrealpa Limestone (Bunyeroo Gorge, Red Hill Well, Mount Billy Creek)
In samples from the Bunyeroo Gorge (AWRA, AWRB) only an A-com-
ponent of reversed polarity was present, which became broken down
between 260°C and 45O’C (Fig. 1.6K). Samples from site AWRC sampled at
Red Hill Well, and also samples from a basal bank at Mount Billy Creek
(BWII) revealed well determinable and internally consistent directions, but
these were distinctly aberrant from the overall B-component direction of the
Wirrealpa Limestone. These directions were discarded, although the reason
for this aberrancy remains obscure. The remaining ten sites of the Wirrealpa
Limestone at Mount Billy Creek (BWIA-BWIK) all showed well-deter-
minable A-component directions of reversed polarity (Fig. 1.5N), which were
broken down between 260°C and 450°C (Fig. 1.6H, T). There is some indica-
tion for a minor blocking temperature range around 350” C.
Aroona Creek Limestone (Mount Scott area)
An A-component and/or a B-component, each with both normal and
reversed polarity, became broken down between 400°C and 650” C (Fig.
1.4B, L, C). When both components were present, the A-component was
broken down generally between 250°C and 400°C and the B-component
between 450°C and 650°C. There was no distinct blocking temperature
range noticeable (Fig. 1.6C), apart from some weak indications between
350” C and 400” C,
Moodlutuna Formation (Red Hill Well, Balcoracana Creek, Mount Billy
Creek)
In the Red Hill Well sites (AMOC, AMOD) a B-component of reversed
polarity became broken down at the higher temperatures up to 670°C (Fig.

### page_22
270
1.6N). Only a few specimens from these sites showed the breakdown of the
A-component of reversed polarity in the same interval. The Balcoracana
Creek sites (AMOA, AMOB), in contrast, showed a pronounced A-compo-
nent, which became broken down between 500°C and 675°C (Fig. 1.50, R,
S,), but a B-component was not well identifiable. Both normal and reversed
polarity directions of this A-component occur in the same specimen (Fig.

The Moodlatana samples from Mount Billy Creek revealed an A-com-
ponent only (Fig. 1.5P, Q) of reversed polarity (through-out) and normal
polarity (middle part only), which became broken down down above 400°C.
All samples showed a distinct blocking temperature range between 630°C
and 670°C with some indication for another less pronounced blocking
temperature range around 500°C (Fig. 1.6M, R).
Balcorucana Formation (Balcoracana Creek)
An A-component of normal (APNB) or reversed polarity (APND) was
broken down separately above 500°C up to 680” C (Fig. 1.5T). Site APNA
and APNC samples showed well concentrating directions of reversed polarity
only, broken down in the same temperature interval (Fig. 1.5U), which
streaked towards the B-component directions as determined from other
formations. All samples revealed a distinct blocking temperature range
between 630°C and 680°C and another less pronounced one at 450-500°C
(Fig. 1.60, P).
Pantupinna Formation (Balcoracana Creek)
A- and B-components both of normal and reversed polarity occur (Fig.
1.5V, W), the latter being the more prominent. The A-component generally
becomes broken down at the higher temperatures in the range 500-67O”C
(Fig. 1.6Q). In some specimens both a normal and reversed polarity of the B-
or A-component were present. Most samples showed a fairly wide blocking
temperature spectrum between 400” C and 670” C (Fig. 1.6Q).
INTERPRETATION
A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate
specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T,
U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis
of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding.
As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is
most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite,
maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a)
dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968;
Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston

### page_23
271
and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be
a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments
(Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972;
Larson and Walker, 1975).
It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may
acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of
exchange coupling with the original magnetic phase or because of a resultant
magnetostatic interaction field from nearby grains. In case of carbonate
samples with a weak initial intensity which are subsequently further reduced
during the demagnetization process, formation of such a secondary magnetic
component may make it impossible to determine the primary magnetic
component. Most red-bed samples showed an increase in susceptibility
(Fig. 1.6R) after prolonged heating at temperatures above 500-6OO”C. A
notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and
from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4),
which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above
400°C. This may be due to inversion of m~haemite to haematite (Turner
and Ixer, 1977).
The individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetiza-
tion was variable (Fig. 1.5). It was often found that specimens taken from
the same sample showed widely different blocking temperature regions for
magnetic components of similar direction. This may partly be due to initial
presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson
and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic
properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976).
Therefore, I prefer to treat the specimen directions as the fundamental unit
for calculation of mean directions, rather than basing this calculation on
sample-mean directions.
As shown before, two characteristic magnetic components have been dis-
tin~ished: (a) a SSW directed component (A) with medium to low upwards
inclination, and (b) a WNW-NNW directed component (B) with a low down-
wards inclination. Normal and reversed polarities of both components occur.
A feature observed throughout this series of studies (Sections I, II, III) was
the appreciable scatter in individual specimen directions, representing one of
the two characteristic magnetic components. Rather than attributing this
phenomenon to inaccuracies in determining individual specimen directions,
this scatter has to be seen as an intrinsic property of the samples, reflecting
a complex magnetization history. Although orthogonal projection figures
are a very powerful tool in interpretation, such an analysis necessarily fails
in case of a multi-component magnetic system with partly overlapping
stability spectra. Clearly, composite breakdown of multicomponent magne-
tizations with variable component ratios throughout a formation, neces-
sarily (1) cont~butes to an enhanced scatter in directions and (2) yields
streaks between the end directions of the various components. In the present
studies (Sections I, II, III) this effect results in a non-Fisherian distribution

### page_24
212
of specimen directions with most of the spread residing in the declination.
The spreads of directions of the two characteristic magnetic components
overlap. Because of the distinct behaviour of each specimen it was virtually
impossible to group the component directions according to their magnetic
characteristics. The best alternative was to subject the directions of individ-
ual specimen components to frequency analysis and to judge mean com-
ponent directions from peaks evident in the frequency distribution. Com-
ponent directions of the individual specimens were then grouped on the basis
of their proximity to one of the dominant directions. Admittedly, this is
a somewhat subjective approach which may statistically enhance the separa-
tion, yielding results farther apart than they are in actuality. However, being
the sole option available, the method tends to be justified as the obtained
mean directions could be interpreted in a meaningful way with respect to the
mean early Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic data from Gondwanaland and the
tectonic and thermo-chemical history of the region studied.
The occasional presence of both normal and reversed polarities of the
same magnetic component in the same specimen (Fig. 1.7A), points to a
fairly long period of acquisition of the characteristic magnetic component
spanning at least the period of one polarity reversal. Such a prolonged
acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic
oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and
oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo-
chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red
clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in
both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. The latter was acquired
with a time lag of several 100.000 yrs due to the effect of changing Eh-Ph
condition in the CRM formation process.
Dual polarity observations were also made in Billy Creek equivalent beds
on Kangaroo Island and in some sequences in the Amadeus Basin (Section
III). In the latter basin, specimens from red beds in a Middle Cambrian
section near Areyonga showed components of dual polarity, whereas
time equivalent rocks of a carbonate sequence near Ross River did not show
this effect. Clearly, such a prolonged period of acquisition of magnetization,
leading occasionally in red beds to a dual polarity, questions the suitability
of such thermally demagnetized red beds results for magnetostratigraphic
studies. Chemical demagnetization may prove to be more successful in those
cases where early and late diagenetic magnetization components can be
separated on the basis of distinct chemical properties (Roy and Park, 1974),
but has not been undertaken in the course of the present study.
A comparison with the mean Gondwanaland data points to the SSW-SW
directed magnetic component (A) as the primary magnetization. Its direc-
tion shows a minor gradual change through the stratigraphical sequence as
will be discussed (Table I.1). I interpret the WNW-NNW aligned charac-
teristic magnetic component (B) as a secondary magnetization which pre-
dates regional folding of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” sediments during the

### page_25
273
Late Cambrian-Early Ordovician Delamarian Orogeny. This is evident from
the positive fold test upon comparison of bedding corrected mean directions
(Table 1.2) from west dipping beds in the western Flinders Ranges (Hawker
Group, Billy Creek Formation, Wirrealpa Limestone) with east dipping beds
from the eastern Flinders Ranges (Billy Creek Formation) and with south-
west dipping beds from the Mount Scott area (Ajax Limestone, Aroona
Creek Limestone). Acquisition of this B-component most probably resulted
from enhanced chemical activity, operating at slightly elevated temperatures.
An early thermal phase predating the main deformative event of the Delama-
rian Orogeny is well reflected in pre- to syntectonically emplaced granites in
the Mount Lofty Ranges and on southern Kangaroo Island during the Late
Cambrian (-+510 m.y.; Mimes et al., 1977), and in pre-deformative new
growth of metamorphic minerals (Fleming and Offler, 1968; Offler and
Fleming, 1968). Closing dates of the isotopic systems suggest that such an
enhanced heat flux might have continued in the southern extreme of the
Adelaide “Geosyncline” for about 50 m.y. into the Late Ordovician.
The interpretation of this B-component as a thermo-chemically induced
secondary magnetic component of Late Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is
further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade
of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn-
cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general
increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”,
with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide
“Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence
of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges.
Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill
beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from
haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic
anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent
magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent
magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc-
tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was
imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the
trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction
of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component
with the characteristic component B is striking. The other secondary mag-
netic component described by McKirdy et al., although not well recognizable
in the present study, may have further attributed to the appreciable scatter
in directions of the characteristic magnetic components. Although the grade
of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges proved to be beyond the
resolving power of McKirdy et al.% method, the present study indicates the
general trend of an increase in metamorphic grade from west to east over
the “Geosyncline” also to be present in the central Flinders Ranges. The
secondary magnetic component B was hardly noticeable in the sections from
the western side of the central Flinders Ranges (Bunyeroo Gorge, Parachilna

### page_26
274
Gorge), but appeared the more evident at the eastern side of the central
Flinders Ranges (Balcoracana Creek, Mount Billy Creek) and in the northern
Flinders Ranges (Aroona Creek).
AS will be elaborated in the following sections (II, III), similar overprints
are Present also in Billy Creek equivalent red beds on Kangaroo Island and
in Middle-Late Cambrian sequences from the Amadeus Basin. In the latter
region, there are no indications for Late Cambrian-E~ly Ordovician oro-
genie activity (Wells et al., 1970; Wells, 1976), so the evident magnetic over-
printing has to be assigned to an as yet unnoticed thermo-chemical event
contemporaneous with the one which affected the Adelaide “Geosyncline”.
Finally, the primary magnetic component A needs some discussion. The
few earlier studies on Cambrian p~aeom~etism of the Adelaide “Geosyn-
cline” (Briden, 1967; Giddings, 1974; Embleton and Giddings, 1974;
Giddings and Embleton, 1976) also point to problems similar to those
encountered in the present study: individuality of the specimens upon
thermal treatment, remagnetization during the Late Cambrian-Early Ordo-
vician times and frequently a high scatter in directions. This prevented
Briden (1967) from obtaining conclusive results for the Billy Creek Forma-
tion. Results mentioned by Embleton and Giddings (1974) for red-bed
sequences of late-Early Cambrian age (Billy Creek Formation), Middie
Cambrian age (lower Lake Frome Group) and of a presumed Late Cambrian
age (upper Lake Frome Group, probably the Grindstone Range Sandstone)
show some similarity to the results obtained during this study. However, the
difficulty in removing the the~o-chemically overprinted component B,
not separated by them, and the large scatter in the few data that remain
after rejections, urge a careful attitude to the numerical data presented in
these studies.
The mean data for the primary magnetization of the Cambrian sequence
of the Flinders Ranges as obtained in this study shows some gradual change
in direction (Figs. 1.7A, B, C) and in pole position (Fig. 1.8). The bulk of the
polar motion recorded in the Flinders Ranges sequences must have taken
place in Early Cambrian times, but unfortunately acceptable data from the
Early Cambrian Hawker Group (Table 1.1) are rare. The few low accuracy
data from the earliest Cambrian Parachilna Formation and from the basal
Wilkawillina Limestone, supported by the Ajax Limestone results, indicate
a gradual move in pole position away from the Late Precambrian-Early
Cambrian quasi-static pole position as recorded in Amadeus Basin sequences
(Kirschvink, 1978a, b), towards a more stable Middle Cambrian pole posi-
tion as indicated by the Billy Creek red beds, the Wirrealpa Limestone-
Aroona Creek Limestone sequences and the Lake Frome Group red beds.
This pattern of movement accords with the Middl~~te Cambrian
data from the Amadeus Basin and from the Billy Creek equivalent of Kanga-
roo Island (Sections II, III), and fits with the general trend of a revised APW
path for Gondwanaland (cf. Figs. 111.13, 15).
The mean result (Table 1.1) for carbonates of the top Hawker Group

### page_27
275

(sites APAG, AORA) and the basal Billy Creek beds (sites APCE, ABCF,
ABCG), is notably out of sequence. The pole position seems to be deflected
towards the Late Cambrian-Early Ordovician pole position corresponding
with the overprinted B-component. It is quite possible that this result
represents a pseudo-stable component due to a composite breakdown of the
SW directed primary component (A) and the NW directed secondary com-
ponent (B). Like the results from the underlying carbonate beds of the
middle Hawker Group, which show composite breakdown of a primary
magnetization component (A) and a recent field component (RFC) (Table
I.l), this result has been discarded.
Another notable observation is the southward deflected declination of the
primary magnetic component in the upper Wirrealpa Limestone-lower
Moodlatana succession sampled at Mount Billy Creek (Table 1.1). The corre-
sponding pole positions (Fig. 1.8) are near to late Precambrian pole positions

### page_29
271
as obtained by Kirschvink (1978a, b) for the Amadeus Basin (cf. Figs. 111.13,
14). The origin of this well observed aberrant set of directions is not clear,
they may possibly represent an excursion of the geomagnetic field.
The upper age limit of the Lake Frome Group sedimentation is not very
well established. According to Daily (in Thompson et al., 1976), sedimenta-
tion in the Adelaide “Geosyncline” ceased with the onset of the Delamarian
Orogeny. Daily (1956) originally suggested a Middle- to possible Late Cam-
brian age for the topmost beds of the Lake Frome Group, successively
revised (Daily, in Thompson et al., 1976) to a possible continuation of sedi-
mentation into the Early Ordovician. A comparison of Lake Frome Group
Data here presented with data of Giddings (1974) and Embleton and
Giddings (1974) for the upper Lake Frome Group beds, with Middle to
Late Cambrian results for the Amadeus Basin (Section III) suggests that
acquisition of magnetization of the Lake Frome Group beds pre-dated
acquisition in the upper part of the Shannon Formation of the Ross River
section. The latter Shannon Formation is of early-Late Cambrian age (Wells
et al., 1970). In the absence of indications that the acquisition of the
primary magnetization of the Shannon beds lagged appreciably behind
sedimentation, there is thus fair reason to assume that the Lake Frome
Group sedimentation did not continue into Late Cambrian times.
CONCLUSIONS
A major problem encountered in this study was the directional interpre-
tation of individual magnetic components. Aberrant directions present, in
particular, in carbonate rocks of the Early Cambrian Hawker Group, have
been interpreted as pseudo-stable directions caused by composite break-
down of various magnetic components.
Three magnetic components have been indentified:
(1) A well recognizable recent field component (RFC) of appreciable
intensity.
(2) A WNW-NNW directed secondary magnetic component (B) of low
downwards inclination.
(3) SSW-SW directed component (A) of medium to low upwards inclina-
tion, interpreted as representing the primary magnetization.
Both latter components were present as normal and reversed polarity
directions. Because of the distinctive behaviour of the specimens during
thermal demagnetization treatment and the appreciable scatter in component
directions, a frequency analysis had to be applied for assignment of compo-
nent directions to either or both groupings.
The secondary magnetic components (B) is interpreted as resulting from
thermochemical activity during a period of regional upheating predating
the diastrophistic phase of the Cambro-Ordovician Delamarian Orogeny.
The primary magnetic component indicates reduced polar motion during
the Middle Cambrian (quasi static interval). The few early Cambrian data

### page_30
available suggests a period of rapid polar motion, during which the pole
moved from its Late Precambrian-Early Cambrian quasi-static position to
its Middle Cambrian quasi-static position.
A comparison of Lake Frome Group palaeomagnetic data with newly
obtained and well dated results from the Amadeus Basin indicates that the
Lake Frome Group sedimentation probably did not continue into Late
Cambrian times.
II. Late Early Cambrian results from Kangaroo Island, South Australia
INTRODUCTION
The peculiar shape of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” (cf. Fig. I.l), sigmoidal
with an added northwards spur of the Flinders Ranges has inspired a number
of widely different genetic models.
Crawford and Campbell (1973a) suggested possible large-scale horizontal
displacement within the Australo-Antarctic assembly during Late Cambrian
and mainly Ordovician times. They postulated two deformation phases to
explain the southwestern bend of the Adelaide “Geosyncline”, supposed
by them to have been aligned originally in a meridional direction. Compression
during the Late Cambrian caused by movement of the Gawler Block,
followed in Early Ordovician times by large scale fault drag of Kangaroo
Island and the Mount Lofty Ranges. This drag was caused by at least 300 km
of dextral movement along a postulated NW-SE aligned shear zone, passing
from the southern extreme of the Gawler Block along northern Tasmania.
By contrast Harrington et al. (1973), supported by Veevers (1976), postu-
lated that sinistral and not dextral movement along a rather similar fault
zone occurred during the middle Palaeozoic, followed by dextral movement
up to 900 km in the late Mesozoic. Harrington et al. agree with convicing
arguments put forward by Daily et al. (1973) that the southwestern bend of
the Adelaide “Geosyncline” is not due to fault drag, but represents
primary depositional trends, around the margin of the stable Gawler Block.
Likewise, large-scale rotations in the northern part of the Adelaide “Geo-
syncline” also postulated by Crawford and Campbell (1973a) were refuted
by Glen et al. (1977) on the grounds of similarity in deformation trends
between the Willyama block and the Gawler Block. Scheibner (1974), like
Crawford and Campbell (1973a, b) was less impressed by the stability of the
Gawler Block, and suggested deformation of the southern Adelaide “Geo-
syncline” by a southeasterly rotation of the Gawler Block during the Late
Cambrian-Early Ordovician Delamarian Orogeny. Other models put forward
by Stewart and Mount (1972), Katz (1976), Dunnet (1976), Coward (1976)
and Stewart (1976) suggest formation of the Adelaide “Geosyncline”
through horizontal displacements for which various magnitudes, various
shear zones and various timings of movement are advanced. Stewart and
Mount (1972), Coward (1976) and Stewart (1976) in particular, suggest a

### page_31
279
relation between a shear zone in the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and a zone of
seismic activity (Doyle et al., 1968; Doyle, 1971; Clearly and Simpson,
1971; Stewart and Mount, 1972), which follows the Adelaide “Geosyncline”
and may be continuable through the Australian continent and southwards
into the Indian Ocean, ultimately reflected in the offset of the Antarctic
Ridge. From electrical conductivity studies, Lilley (1975) describes an
evident conductor zone in the northern Flinders and mentions ductile shear
as a possible cause for enhanced electrical conductivity. Although this con-
ductor is displaced eastwards with respect to the zone of seismic activity,
it may well be related to the various N-NNW trending shear zones suggested
by Stewart and Mount (1972), Coward (1976), Stewart (1976) and Glen
et al. (1977).
Palaeomagnetic studies may provide some constraints to the many widely
divergent hypotheses for the development of the Adelaide Orogenic zone,
with most of them postulating some kind of rotational or translational
movements. Small differential movements along a shear zone which may have
been slightly oblique to the Cambro-Ordovician palaeolatitude pattern
(cf. Fig. 111.13) are beyond the current resolution of the palaeomagnetic
method, and are also difficult to test on geological ground (Glen et al.,
1977). Associated rotations, however, can often be detected palaeomagne-
tically.
Only a few palaeomagnetic results for the southern part of the Adelaide
“Geosyncline” have previously been published. McWilliams (1977) noted
a discrepancy between results by Karner (1975) from the Brachina Forma-
tion (Wilpena Group, late Proterozoic) collected near Hallett Cove, south
of Adelaide and his own data from the Brachina Formation of the central
Flinders Ranges, but he was unable to interpret this discrepancy in accord-
ance with existing models for deformation of the Adelaide “Geosyncline”.
Unnoted by McWilliams, there is a marked similarity between results
obtained by Briden (1967) from Marinoan sediments sampled near Hallett
Cove (decl. = 191”, incl. = +39”), and a result obtained by McWilliams
(1977) for the Yerelina subgroup (decl. = 184”, incl. = +33”) sampled in the
northern Flinders Ranges. Such a similarity implies no rotational deforma-
tion of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” since the late Proterozoic. McWilliams
preferred, however, to interpret hos own results as a secondary overprint.
Briden’s (1967) results from a late-Early Cambrian sequence on Kangaroo
Island, similar to the sequence studied in this paper, are not useful for a
comparison with other areas of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” because of the
reported difficulty in isolating the primary magnetization. Giddings and
Embleton (1974, 1976) obtained comparable palaeomagnetic directions for
Proterozoic dyke systems from Yorke Peninsula and from Eyre Peninsula,
and therefore refuted Crawford’s hypothesis of large-scale horizontal dis-
placements and associated faultdrag in southern Australia. Crawford and
Campbell (197313) subsequently acknowledged the stability of Yorke Penin-
sula with respect to the Gawler Block. It can be argued, however, that

### page_32
280
Gidding and Embleton’s palaeomagnetic results from Yorke Peninsula may
not be representative for the Kangaroo Island-Mount Lofty Range segment
of the Adelaide “Geosyncline”, as these areas are separated by the Torrens
Lineament which divides the Gawler Block from the more mobile Adelaide
“Geosyncline”.
Further palaeomagnetic testing of genetic models for the Adelaide “Geo-
syncline” is clearly desirable. Well documented data from the Cambrian
of the Flinders Ranges (Section I) and from the Amadeus Basin (Section III)
have been obtained in the course of this project, and palaeomagnetic
research on the Mount Lofty Range-Kangaroo Island arc was initiated as a
natural extension to these studies.
The late-Early Cambrian red-bed sequences on northeastern Kangaroo
Island is correlated by Daily (in Thompson et al., 1976) on fauna1 evidence
with the Billy Creek Formation of the Flinders Ranges. The former sequence
was only mildly affected during the Delamarian Orogeny. Therefore, a study
of this sequence has been undertaken and the results are reported here.
GEOLOGICAL SETTING
Shallow-water-type rocks of late-Early Cambrian age, which are correlated
with paralic deposits of the Billy Creek Formation of the Flinders Ranges
(Fig. 1.2) are exposed over the central northern part of Kangaroo Island
(Fig. II.l), and are known in the subsurface of adjacent Yorke Peninsula
(Stuart and Von Sanden, 1972). The main southern part of the island is
made up by metasediments of the Kanmantoo Group and the underlying
Precambrian. The Flysch-type Kanmantoo sediments form the deep-water
facies equivalent of the shelf type sediments to the north. Deposition of
both facies took place in response to the episodic Kangarooian movements
(Daily, 1956; Daily and Forbes, 1969; Wopfner in Parkin, 1969), i.e.,
the Waitpingan subsidence in the Kanmantoo trough and the associated
Cassinian uplift in the region far to the northeast.
Recent subsurface data have indicated continuation of this sedimentary
basin (Stuart and Von Sanden, 1972; Smith and Kamerling, 1969) along the
southern Gawler Block. An eastwards continuation of the east-west trending
belt of Kanmantoo Group sediments is well recognizable on Fleurieu Penin-
sula and in the Mount Lofty Ranges (Daily, 1969). Subsurface data (B.P.
Thompson, in Parkin, 1969) suggest the presence of Kanmantoo Group
sediments also in the Murray Basin and in western Victoria. From Kangaroo
Island and the continental shelf to the south of it, these Kanmantoo Group
sediments may continue in WNW direction through the offshore Duntrone
basin (Smith and Kamerling, 1969), which follows the southern margin of
the Gawler Block. To the south and west of the Gawler Block beds were
identified which are tentatively correlated with the Billy Creek Formation
and the Lake Frome Group of the Flinders Ranges.
Major fault zones, like the Torrens Lineament, appear to follow the trend

of this sedimentary basin and seem to sweep around the Gawler Block
(Stuart and Von Sanden, 1972; Daily et al., 1973). This contrasts with an
earlier interpretation (Tectonic map of Australia and New Guinea, 1971)
that the N-S aligned Torrens Lineament abuts against the E-W trending
Cygnet-Snelling fault zone on Kangaroo Island (Fig. II.lA). This Cygnet-
Snelling fault zone abruptly separates the undisturbed Billy Creek equivalent
beds of Northern Kangaroo Island from the Kanmantoo Group metasedi-
ments to the south and can be interpreted (Stuart and Von Sanden, 1972)
as the westward continuation of a fault zone swinging from the Mount Lofty

### page_34
282
Ranges along the north coast of the Fleurieu Peninsula towards Kangaroo
Island, and possibly beyond.
The trend of the Cygnet-Snelling fault is well reflected in the meta-
morphic zonation of Kangaroo Island (Offler and Fleming, 1968, Fig. II.lC)
which originated during the Late Cambrian-Early Ordovician Delamarian
Orogeny. Metamorphism up to the andalusite-staurolite facies is recogniz-
able to the south of this fault zone only. Lower-grade metamorphism in
biotite facies occurs further to the north, whereas the well exposed Cam-
brian sequence along the north coast has been affected up to the chlorite
facies only. Sampling has been restricted, therefore, to this region only (Fig.
IISD).

### page_35
SAMPLING LOCALITIES
A conformable sequence of late-Early Cambrian strata, about 1500 m
thick, is well exposed in the cliff section north of Mount Marsden (Fig.
II.lD), between Bald Rock on the eastern side of Emu Bay and White Point
at the western extreme of Boxing Bay. A total of seventeen sites (108 block
samples) of at least six samples each has been sampled through the lower
1200 m of this sequence (Table 11.1). All samples were orientated in the
field with both a magnetic and a solar compass, using a device analoguous
to that described by Embleton and Edwards (1973).
Four formations have been sampled along this profile (Fig. II.lD, Table
11.1):
(A) One site (AKIR) has been collected in the lowermost sampled forma-
tion the Smith Bay Shale in a red to purple quartzitic sandstone (AKIR)
and micaceous shale sequence which forms the 120 m thick upper member
of this 150 m thick formation.
(B) Eight sites (AKIL-AKIQ and AKIS) have been sampled in reddish
shale and sandstone intercalations (occasionally quartzitic) in the overlying
about 400 m thick White Point Conglomerate.
(C) Another four sites were taken in the conformably overlying Emu
Bay Shale Formation, about 100 m thick. Two sites (AKIG, AKIH) were
sampled in silicified dark greenish thin bedded micaceous shales, silts and
sandstones, which form the upper part of this formation. Two other sites
(AKII, AKIK) were sampled in medium to coarse-grained reddish sand-
stone banks in the basal part of the formation.
(D) Six sites (AKIA-AKIF) were taken through the basal 550 m of the
overlying Boxing Bay Formation, in red to reddish feldspathic medium to
coarse-grained quartzitic sandstones with evident cross bedding.
LABORATORY TREATMENT AND RESULTS
Treatment in the laboratory was essentially the same as described in the
Flinders Ranges study (Section I). At least three cores were taken from each
block sample using a drill press. Two specimens from each site were subjected
to progressive thermal demagnetization in fifteen steps up to 685” C. Remain-
ing specimens, two from each sample, were subjected to partial progressive
thermal demagnetization in nine steps between 300°C and 675°C. Such an
elaborate demagnetization procedure was necessary because of the individual
behaviour of specimens upon thermal cleaning as had been noted also for
comparable rocks of the Flinders Ranges and the Amadeus Basin (Sections I
and III, respectively). Care was taken to keep the specimens in low field
magnetic environments to prevent excessive build up of viscous remanent
magnetization (VRM). All magnetic measurements were carried out on a
computerized ScT 2-axis superconducting rock magnetometer, and suscepti-
bility measurements were taken on a Digico bulk susceptibility unit. Direc-

phenomenon was noticed particularly in samples from the dark g-rey shale
horizons of sites AKIG and AKIH (Fig. II_4A-F).
The intensity decay curves in general show two distinct blocking temper-
ature ranges (Fig. 11.5A, B, E-K). A lower one between 500°C and 6OO”C,
probably associated with a magnetite phase, and a higher one between
650°C and 675” C, characteristic of haematite, However, a number of
samples show a wider distribution of blocking temperatures (Fig. II.5C, D).
AI1 samples except those from the aberrant Emu Bay Shales (AKIG, AKIH),
decreased in susceptibility between 300°C and 500°C (Fig. II.5L-_N, Q-U),
which is probably due to inversion of maghaematite into haematite (Turner
and Ixer, 1977). Both this dual blocking temperature range and the decrease
in susceptibility upon heating are found also in the correlated Billy Creek
Formation of the Flinders Ranges (Fig. 1.6s).
Similar to the general magnetization pattern of the Flinders Ranges
samples, two characteristic magnetic components have been identified:
(1) A SSW-WSW directed magnetic component (A) with low upwards dip
(Fig. 11.3A).
(2) A WNW-NNW directed magnetic component (B) with low downwards
dip (Fig. 11.3B).
Normal and reversed polarity directions of both components are present.
Similar to the Flinders Ranges samples (Section I) different specimens
showed a highly variable behaviour of the two characteristic magnetic
components during thermal demagnetization. No correlation at all could be
established between the two prevalent blocking temperature ranges and the
two characteristic magnetic components. For these reasons and also because
of the dual polarity representation of both characteristic components, it
was occasionally not possible to attribute somewhat deviating magnetic
directions, though very evident on the orthogonal demagnetization graphs,
to either the B-component or the A-component grouping. It is possible that
such directions represent pseudo-stable artefacts resulting from composite
breakdown, at constant ratios, of two or more magnetic components. Con-
sequently such directions have been discarded from the statistical analysis,
which was based on analysis of frequency distribution plots (Fig. II.3A, B)
as detailed elsewhere (Section I}.
In a number of specimens throughout the sampled section (Fig. 11.4,6, K,
I+ M, 0), both a normal polarity direction (cleaned at 400-600”C) and a
reversed polarity direction (cleaned at 600480” C) of the A-component
were present. This peculiar phenomenon, also observed in red-bed sequences
from the Flinders Ranges (Section I) and the Amadeus Basin (Section III),
points to a prolonged period of magnetization acquisition upon diagenesis.
Findings of both normal and reversed polarity directions of the RFC in
especially the Emu Bay Shale Formation suggests a Simih acquisition of
more recent origin.
clearly this observation seriously limits the use of these thermally demag-
netized red beds results for magnetostratigraphic purposes.

INTERPRETATION
Figure 11.6B shows that both the normal and the reversed polarity direc-
tion of the (RFC) are in good agreement with the virtual direction at the
sampling locality according to the axial geocentric dipole field model, but
not with the present local field direction (Table 11.1). This RFC must have
been acquired during a prolonged period of fairly recent weathering, prob-
ably of latest Cainozoic age, which spanned at least one polarity reversal.
Extensively laterized surfaces are present on Kangaroo Island and on
adjacent areas of South Australia, and widely different ages ranging from
Early Mesozoic (Daily et al., 1974) to Plio-Pleistocene (Northcote, 1946;
Sprigg, 1955; Major and Vitals, 1973) have been suggested for this lateriza-
tion period. Schmidt (1976, also in Schmidt et al., 1976) discerned a magne-
tization component of both normal and reversed polarity in some laterite
samples from Kangaroo Island, which he correlated with secondary magnetic
components found in the Springfield Basin of the Flinders Ranges and in the
Perth Basin (Schmidt, 1976). Comparison of their pole positions with the
Tertiary apparent polar wander path for Australia (Wellmann et al., 1969;
Fig. 11.6. Equal area projection of mean directions, see Table 11.1. A. Site mean direc-
tion of the primary magnetic component (A). B. Mean directional results from the

secondary magnetic component (S), compared with the mean late-Early-srly-Middle
Cambrian results of the Flindem Ranges (inverted triangles). Square (DF) is the virtual
direction at the sample locality according to the axial geocentric dipole field model.
Hexagon (PF) is the present field direction at the sampling loeali~. Recent field com-
ponent directions: N = normal polarity, R = reversed polarity, R = swapped reversed
polarity.

### page_42
290
McElhinny et al., 197413) led him to interpretation of his results (Schmidt,
1976; Schmidt et al., 1976) in terms of a dominant period of lateritic
weathering during Late Oligocene-Early Miocene times which affected
a large area of Australia (Woolnough, 1927). It should be mentioned, how-
ever, that Schmidt’s interpretation of a Middle Tertiary remagnetization
component, if correct, merely points to one specific episode in a possible
complex remagnetization history and does not at all nullify suggestions for
an older, possible early Mesozoic, phase of laterization as proposed by Daily
et al. (1974).
The RFC directions found in the present study correspond with a pole
position which is removed from the middle Tertiary segment of Australia’s
APW, and Schmidt et al’s (1976) laterite results from Kangaroo Island
are in fact similarly removed (Fig. 111.11). In contrast, the agreement of this
RFC with the virtual “dipole field” direction (Fig. ILGA, Table II.l),
suggests a latest Cainozoie period of acquisition,
The northwestwards directed and slightly downwards dipping B-com-
ponent of both normal and reversed polarity (Fig. 11.4N-S 11.6B) can be
correlated after correction for bedding with a similar secondary magnetic
component found in the Flinders Ranges (Section I) and in the Amadeus
Basin (Section III). As detailed before (Section I), this secondary magnetic
component must have been induced by thermo-chemical activity prior to
the main folding phases of the Delamarian Orogeny. Detailed studies of meta-
morphic crystallization in the Mount Lofty Ranges (Fleming and Offler,
1968; Offler and Fleming, 1968; Milnes et al., 1977) identify three folding
phases during the Delamarian Orogeny. Although intensive metamorphism
and widespread granite intrusion, attributed to an unusually high heat flow
from the mantle, commenced before the first folding phase (Offler and
Fleming, 1968): synte~tonic metamorphism and the non-closure of isotopic
systems (Milness et al., 197’7) indicate a maybe only locally prolonged period
(at least 50 m.y.) of elevated temperatures. It is possible that a minor part
of this B-component was acquired during a later stage of the Delamarian
Orogeny and thus postdates one or more of the three folding phases. In the
absence of any detailed knowledge about the magnetization-deformation
relationship for the sampled Kangaroo Island beds, it was only possible to
correct for the total accumulated dip. This simple correction procedure
might be one of the reasons for the appreciable scatter in component direc-
tions.
The southw~ds directed and slightly upwards inclined A-component, of
both normal and reversed polarity (Fig. 11.4A, G-O, 11.6& Table II.l),
agrees after correction for bedding with the mean primary magnetic direc-
tion of the correlated Billy Creek Formation of the Flinders Ranges, and is
thought to represent the primary magnetization direction. B. Daily (in
Thompson et al., 1976) correlated the studied sequence with the late-Early
Cambrian Billy Creek Formation of the Flinders Ranges on the grounds of
similarity in lithology and in fauna. This correlation is supported by the

### page_43
291
observed similarity in magnetic characteristics, similar dual blocking temper-
ature range, decrease of susceptibility upon heating, and an apparently
prolonged period of acquisition of magnetization as evidenced by the
presence of both normal and reversed polarities in some specimens. This
points to an identical source of sediment and a similar depositional eviron-
ment. Although the late-Early to Middle Cambrian has been identified as a
period of rather slow polar motion (Sections I and III), which reduces the
resolution of any attempted palaeo-directional correlation, the good agree-
ment in primary magnetic directions from the studied Kangaroo Island
ADELAIDE “GEOSYNCLINE” RESULTS
Fig. 11.7. Newly obtained palaeomagnetic S-pole positions for the Cambrian of Kangaroo
Island, compared with new results from the Flinders Ranges (Section I), superimposed

### page_44
292
sequence and from the Billy Creek Formation of the Flinders Ranges adds
further support to this correlation (Fig. 11.6A, B).
Neglecting the danger of circular reasoning, it may equally well be stated
that the agreement of both the primary magnetic direction (late-Early
Cambrian) and the slightly younger secondary magnetic directions from the
Flinders Ranges with those from Kangaroo Island (Fig. II.GB, 7), virtually
exclude any rotations movement between both areas since late-Early
Cambrian times. On the basis of available palaeomagnetic data it is not
possible, however, to exclude the possibility of rotational movements in
other areas of the Adelaide “Geosyncline”. The agreement between Briden’s
(1967) results for Marinoan sediments from Hallett Cove (Mount Lofty
Ranges) and McWilliams (1977) result for the Yerelina subgroup from the
northern Flinders Ranges on the one hand, and the discrepancy between
Karner’s (1975) results for the Brachina Formation from Hallett Cove and
McWilliam’s results for the Brachina Formation from the Central Flinders
Ranges on the other hand, needs further testing in this respect.
Further palaeomagnetic data are needed also to test various hypotheses
suggesting ~~slation~ movement along megashear zones in the Adelaide
“Geosyncline” and along the southeast Australian shelf. The suggested
magnitude of some of these movements and their oblique position with
respect to the palaeolatitude pattern (cf. Fig. 111.14) possibly falls within the
resolution of the palaeomagnetic method.
CONCUSSIONS
The magnetization pattern of the late-Early Cambrian red-bed sequence
on northeastern Kangaroo Island appeared to be similar to the magnetiza-
tion history of penecontemporaneous sequences in the Flinders Ranges
(Section I) and in the Amadeus Basin (Section III).
Three magnetic components have been identified:
(a) A recent magnetic component (RFC) of both normal and reversed
polarity, with a direction very near to the virtual “dipole field” direction at
the sample locality.
(b) A northwestwards directed and slightly downwards inclined secondary
magnetic component (B) of both normal and reversed polarity. This magne-
tization originated largely before the main folding phases of the Delamarian
Orogeny and most probably was induced by enhanced thermo-chemical
activity which commenced before the diastrophistic phases of the Delama-
rian Orogeny. This activity may have persisted for a fairly long period and
acquisition of an unquantified but probably minor part of this magnetization
may have continued during the later folding phases, The correction applied
here for total accumulated dip of the beds may have attributed to the
appreciable scatter in directions.
(c) A southwestwards directed and slightly upwards inclined magnetic
component (A) of both normal and reversed polarity, which has been

### page_45
293
identified as the primary magnetization. A prolonged period of acquisition
of magnetization upon diagenesis is indicated by the presence of both
normal and reversed polarities of this component in the same specimens.
Similar observations were made also on the primary magnetic content of
Cambrian red beds from the Flinders Ranges (Section I) and from the
Amadeus Basin (Section III) and may limit the applicability of these
thermally demagnetized red beds for magnetostratigraphic purposes.
The directional agreement of both the primary magnetic component (A)
and the secondary magnetic component (B) in the beds under study with a
similar magnetization pattern in the correlated Billy Creek Formation of the
Flinders Ranges, indicates absence of relative rotational movement between
Kangaroo Island and the northwestern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline”,
since late-Early Cambrian times. More palaeomagnetic data are needed,
however, to further test various models postulating shear in the Adelaide
“Geosyncline” and along southeast Australia’s shelf.
III. Middle to early-Late Cambrian results from the Amadeus Basin
(Northern Territory)
INTRODUCTION
Palaeomagnetic studies on Cambrian rocks from the Adelaide “Geosyn-
cline” (Sections I and II) have met with considerable difficulties in separat-
ing the primary magnetic component from a dominant recent field compo-
nent and from another thermochemically induced secondary component
of Cambro-Ordovician age. Interpretation of results was not straightforward,
and complementary information from other sequences of Cambrian age in
Australia was needed. Therefore, a study on the Amadeus Basin succession
was undertaken. Additional objectives were:
(1) Better definition of the Cambrian part of the Australian apparent
polar wanderpath (APW), for which rapid polar motion has been inferred
before (Embleton, 1972a, b; McElhinny and Embleton, 1974, 1976;
McElhinny et al., 1974b).
(2) Study of possible intraplate tectonics as suggested amongst others by
Harrington et al. (1973).
(3) Identification of palaeomagnetic constraints on age ranges of unfossili-
ferous formations through intracontinental comparison of magnetostrati-
graphic records and pole positions.
(4) Comparison of palaeomagnetic characteristics in a heterotopical
facies environment as typical for the Amadeus Basin.
(5) Intercontinental correlation of polarity sequences.
The Amadeus Basin (Fig. 111.1) forms a natural object for a palaeomagne-
tic study. Outcrop is good, and the structural and stratigraphical history of
the basin is well known from extensive regional mapping as compiled by
Wells et al. (1970) and Wells (1976). It is therefore not surprising that

### page_46
294
Australian palaeomagnetic workers paid special attention to a study of the
Amadeus Basin. Embleton (1972a, b) initiated palaeomagnetic research in
this basin with a study of some formations from the Ellery Creek succession
(Fig. 111.3).
More extensive studies were recently finalised by McWilliams (1977) on
late Proterozoic rocks and by Kirschvink (1978a, b) on several successions
spanning the Precambrian-Cambrian boundary period. So the earlier part of
the sedimentation record of the Amadeus Basin seems fairly well established.
The present study of two Middle--early-Late Cambrian successions in the
Amadeus Basin was carried out in cooperation with Kirschvink’s (1978a, b)
magnetostratigraphic analysis of the Precambrian-Cambrian boundary
period. To enhance mutual compatibility and moreover to detail a suggested
rapid polar motion (Embleton, 1972a, b; McElhinny and Embleton, 1974,
1976; McElhinny et al., 1974b) a detailed sampling at regular intervals
throughout the formations was pursued in this study.
GEOLOGICAL SETTING
The Amadeus Basin in Central Australia is an east-west aligned intra-
cratonic depression stretching over about 800 km from the southern part of
the Northern Territory into West Australia (Fig. 111.1). A 9000-m thick
sedimentation record spanning a period from late Proterozoic to late Palaeo-
zoic is preserved in the basin (see, for a description, Wells et al., 1970 and
Wells, 1976). Sedimentation started no more than 1000 m.y. ago with
blanket deposits, and became more localized with the onset of three late
Proterozoic diastrophistic movements. The latest Proterozoic-earliest
Cambrian Petermann Ranges Orogeny was the most severe of these diastro-
phistic movements as is evident from large scale folding, nappe movements
and metamorphism along the southern basin margin. These three movements
resulted in uplift of the areas in the south which became the main
provenance for Cambrian sediments that poured into the subsiding area in
to the north. Variable ratios of subsidence in the basin and the localized
sediment source in the southwest resulted during Cambrian times in hetero-
topical facies conditions. Coarse-grained sediments were deposited close to
the uplifted area, grading in north and northeast direction into sandstone,
shale (some marine) and carbonate rocks (i.e. the Eninta Sandstone, Tempe
Formation, Illara Sandstone, Deception Formation and Petermann Sand-
stone, Fig. 111.2). This sequence of predominantly elastic sediments became
much thinner developed in a less subsided north--south zone near the centre
of the basin. In the northeastern part of the basin, carbonate sedimentation
became dominant after deposition of the Arumbera Sandstone; the basal
formation of the Pertaoorta Group (Fig. 11.2). This Group further includes
(Fig. 111.2) carbonate rocks (Todd River Dolomite) tectonically reduced
evaporites (Chandler Limestone), penesaline and marine stromatolitic
carbonates (Giles Creek Dolomite, Shannon Formation) and calcareous silt

### page_47
295
