and silty sands (Goyder Formation). The Arumbera Sandstone (which spans
the Precambiran-Cambrian boundary period (Daily, 1972a; Kirschvink,
1978a)) and the Goyder Formation show minor facies changes only and are
well continuable throughout the basin.
Age control on the sampled parts of the Cambrian successions is rather
well established in the carbonate sequence of the eastern Amadeus Basin
(Ross River section), but is sparse in the arenitic sequence (Areyonga sec-
tion) from the central and western part of the basin. In the Areyonga sec-
tion, the upper part of the Tempe Formation is dated as early-Middle Cam-
brian on the basis of a brachiopod-trilobite-hyolithid-gastropod fauna. No
fauna is known from the underlying Eninta Sandstone, nor in the overlying
Illara Sandstone and the Deception Formation, but Middle Cambrian ages
have been inferred for both latter formations on the basis of their strati-
graphical position underneath the Petermann Sandstone, The latter is ten-
tatively dated as a late-Middle-early-Late Cambrian on the basis of a sparse
gastropod fauna. In the Ross River section, the Giles Creek Dolomite is

dated as early-Middle Cambrian on basis of a hyolithid-brachiopod-
gas~opod-trilobite fauna, whereas the underlying Todd River Dolomite is
dated as Early Cambrian mainly on basis of ~chaeocyathans and brachio-
pods. The overlying Shannon Formation contains a stromatolite fauna,
characteristic for a late Mindyallan age (early-Late Cambrian). Three Palaeo-
zoic movements have occurred (Wells et al., 1970; Wells, 1976) which
mainly affected the northern part of the Basin, in contrast to the late
Proterozoic movements, which mainly affected its southern part. This
resulted from the Cambr~-Ordovician boundary period onwards in south-
wards transgressive sedimentation, intermittent with successive uplifts (the
Rodingan Movement of Silurian age and the Late Devonian Pertnjara Move-
ment), which came to an end with the onset of the Late Devonian-Early
Carboniferous Alice Springs Orogeny.
Most of the folding of the Amadeus Basin occurred during the Alice
Springs Orogeny, which resulted also in large-scale Nappe structures and
resetting of isotopic systems in the area directly to the northeast of the
basin. The Amadeus Basin remained stabilized after this deformation.
Epeirogenic movements brought the area close to submergence in Permian

### page_49
297
and in Mesozoic times. Minor crustal movements occurred during the
Tertiary with erosion and weathering attributing to the present relief.
SAMPLES SECTIONS
Core samples, obtained with a portable drill, were oriented in the field
with both a magnetic and a solar compass, using a device described by
Embleton and Edwards (1973). Samples were taken in the form of magneto-
stratigraphic profiles, either with each sample taken from a separate bed at
regular intervals of generally less than 2 m (Deception Formation, Giles
Creek Dolomite), or in the case of very thick formations, with a greater
interval after each sixth sample (Tempe Formation, Illara Sandstone, Shan-
non Formation). Stratigraphic intervals were measured with a Jacob’s Staff
and an attached Abney level.
For comparison of palaeoma~etic characteristics in time-equiv~ent
sections of different lithology, a late-E~ly-diddle Cambrian red-bed
sequence has been sampled at Areyonga (Fig. 111.3, central Amadeus Basin)
and a Middle--early-Late Cambrian carbonate sequence at Ross River
(eastern Amadeus Basin, Fig. 111.3).
(A) Areyongu section
This section was sampled at the northern head of the Areyonga Gorge
(132.27”E 24.10”5, Fig. 111.3) which dissects the WNW-ESE trending
Gardiner Range anticline; a north-vergent structure with a locally reduced
northern limb. An en-echelon set of north-south trending transverse faults
is well developed at the Areyonga Gorge, but the various formations can
easily be followed in the field.
A Middle Cambrian sequence (Tempe Formation, Illara Sandstone, Decep-
tion Formation), possibly starting already in the latest-Early Cambrian, has
been sampled in the steeply southwards dipping (50-80”) southern limb of
the anticlinal structure.
Tempe Formutio~. In the streambed of the Areyonga Creek, a total of
77 samples (13 sites) has been taken over a strati~aphic sequence of 228 m,
starting about 60 m above the top of the underlying Eninta Sandstone.
Samples were mainly taken in red to reddish coloured siltstones and in addi-
tion in some red dolomites and greyish greenish glauconitic sandstone.
Illara Sandstone. The uppermost part of this formation has been sampIed
in a small ridge to the east of the streambed, as the streambed section itself
seemed reduced by transverse faulting. Twenty-six samples (4 sites), span-
ning a stratigraphic interval of 22 m, have been taken in crossbedded reddish
sandstones.
Deception Formation, This formation consists mainly of reddish mica-
ceous crossbedded sandstones, siltstones and shales and becomes easily
eroded. A total of 63 samples has been taken in the streambed at regular
intervals through the top 148 m of the formation,

(B) Ross River set tion
The eastern closure of a WSW-ENE trending brachy-syncline, made up
by the Pertaoorta Group, is well exposed in the Ross River Gorge (134.49”E
23,62”S, Fig. 111.3). The Alice Springs Orogeny has had a major effect on the
structure of this area as is well reflected in the development of the Arltunga
Nappe Complex directly to the north (Wells et al., 1970; Wells, 1976).
Evaporite sequences from the late Proterozoic Bitter Springs Formation and
from the Early Cambrian Chandler Limestone may have acted as decolle-
ment horizons with a complicated thrust zone connecting both. Mass move-
ment was southwards directed, but no palaeomagnetic indications have been
found so far (Kirschvink, 1978a, b) that such a translational movement was
accompanied by noticeable rotational movement.
A section through the Giles Creek Dolomite and the overlying Shannon
Formation was sampled in the northern part of the Ross River Gorge in the
WNW dipping northern limb of the Ross River syncline.
Giles Creek Dolomite. This formation which consists of dolomite with
interbeds of limestone, siltstone and shale, has been sampled in two over-
lapping sequences. A total of 41 samples (AGCCl-41) has been taken
through mottled to nodular dark grey dolomitic limestones over a strati-
graphic interval of 71 m, from the basalmost exposed beds till about 18 m
below the base of a massive dolomitic limestone member which forms a
very prominent ridge in the terrain. An overlapping sequence of twelve
samples (AGCC42-53) have been drilled through another 23 m thick section
of mottled dolomitic limestone at the base of the massive cliff, and a further
61 samples (AGCC54-102, ASHAl-5, ASHBl-7) have been cored higher up
over a stratigraphic interval of 168 m through massive light coloured bio-
stromal dolomitic limestone, up to the top of the formation.
Shannon Formation. Detailed sampling of this formation, which com-
prises siltstones, limestones and shales, was impractical because of its thick-
ness; so a total of 48 samples (8 sites) were spread over a total stratigraphic
interval of 347 m up to the top of the formation. All cores were drilled in
predominantly massive white bluish dolomitic limestone beds and in yellow
coloured dolomite beds.

LABORATORY TREATMENT AND RESULTS
Laboratory treatment and directional analysis was essentially the same as
described in the Flinders Ranges study (Section I). At least two specimens
from each site, or in the case of a detailed stratigraphic profile one specimen
from each third sample, were subjected to progressive thermal demagnetiza-
tion studies. Red-bed specimens were demagnetized in fifteen steps up to
685°C and carbonate specimens in thirteen steps up to a maximum temper-
ature of 565°C. All remaining red-bed specimens, except those from the
Illara Sandstone (to be discussed) were partially progressively demagnetized
in nine steps between 300” C and 675” C, whereas all remaining carbonate
specimens were demagnetized in six to eleven steps between 150°C and
460°C. Such an elaborate demagnetization procedure was necessary as each
specimen reacted individually upon thermal treatment. This feature has been
noted also in the accompanying studies on rocks from the Adelaide “Geo-
syncline” (Sections I and II). Care was taken to keep the specimens in very
low magnetic fields in order to reduce excessive build up of viscous remanent
magnetization (VRM) after treatment at the higher temperature steps. The
VRM nevertheless prevented continued thermal analysis of the carbonate
specimens above 450” C.
In general, four magnetic components could be identified. A recent field
component (RFC) and three characteristic magnetic components (ASO, B
and A) which are interpreted as predating the main folding phase of the
Early Carboniferous Alice Springs Orogeny.
The recent field component (RFC) was present in all specimens and
dominated the initial directions (Fig. 111.4.1). The AS0 components in SSW
directed with a steep downward dip. Reversed polarity directions of the
component were dominant in the Ross River section (Fig. 111.4.1.), but both
normal and reversed polarity directions of this ASO-component were present
in the Areyonga section, although of a less dominant occurrence (Fig.
111.4.1). The B-component is NW directed with a low downward (Areyonga
section) to low upward (Ross River section) inclination. Both normal and
reversed polarity directions occur (Fig. 111.4.3). The A-component is SW
(Giles Creek Dolomite and Areyonga section) to E (Shannon Formation)
directed with a low upwards inclination, and is also present with normal
and reversed polarities (Fig. 111.4.2).
As will be detailed, the AS0 component is thought to be associated with
the Alice Springs Orogeny, and the A-component is identified as the primary
magnetic component. The B-component is very similar to a secondary mag-
netic component consistently present in samples from the Adelaide “Geo-
syncline” (Sections I and II), which was interpreted before as a result of
thermo-chemical activity during a Late Cambrian-Early Ordovician period
of regional heating.

(A) Areyonga section
Tempe Formation. An RFC of 39-90% of the initial intensity was broken
down completely at 300°C (Fig. 111.5, 7). In some specimens another recent
field component resided in magnetic domains with blocking temperatures
above 600°C (Fig. 111.6). An AS0 component of both normal and reversed
polarity was present in a few samples only (Fig. IILSB). The normal polarity
AS0 component was broken down between 470°C and 64O”C, whereas the
reversed polarity ASO c:omponent became eliminated at slightly lower

temperatures. The secondary B-component is ubiquitous, mostly as reversed
polarity directions. The primary A-component is less well developed; normal
polarity directions predominate at the basal part of the sequence and
reversed polarity directions do so higher up. An evident blocking temper-
ature range between 500°C and 57O”C, attributed to a magnetite phase, and
a less evident blocking range at 650-67O”C, attributed to haematite, are
well visible on the normalized intensity decay curves (Fig. 111.7). A number
of specimens, however, show a wide blocking temperature spectrum with
gradual magnetic breakdown above 500°C. It was not possible to identify
breakdown of the A- or B-component with either of these blocking ranges,
although the A-component becomes mainly broken down at the lower
temperature range and the B-component at the higher temperatures. Spec-
imens from the lower part of the section showed a susceptibility decrease
between 300” and 500°C (Fig. 111.8). With the onset of glauconite higher
up in the sedimentation record, this characteristic changed to a distinct
susceptibility increase after heating above 550” C.
Illura Sandstone. Initial intensities of these samples (Table 111.1) were up
to two orders of magnitude higher than those from samples of the Tempe
Formation and the Deception Formation, sampled in the same Areyonga
section. Initial directions were widely spread and did not reveal the
dominant influence of an RFC, being so prominent in the other formations
studied. The normalized intensity decay curves showed an evident blocking
temperature range between 500°C and 570°C with another less pronounced
blocking temperature range between 650” C and 670°C (Fig. 111.7). In con-
trast, the orthogonal demagnetization graphs showed breakdown of an
essentially mono-component magnetic system with hardly any indication
for a RFC, so dominant elsewhere. As the samples were taken on a ridge,
lightning effects were sus‘pected to be present. For this reason, the remainder
of the specimens were subjected first to alternating field demagnetiza-
tion in seven steps up to 125 mT, followed by partial progressive thermal
demagnetization in eleven steps between 200°C and 675” C. In most spec-
imens, except from state AILC, the AF-demagnetization resulted in
breakdown, largely below 30 mT, of a distinct magnetic component with

strong affinity to either a normal or reversed polarity RFC component or to
the primary A-component (Fig. 111.6). Continued thermal demagnetization
generally resulted in breakdown of a normal or reversed polarity B-com-
ponent, whereas especially in sites AILC and AILD a normal and reversed
A-component became broken down in addition (Fig. 111.6). It can thus be
concluded that the abnormally high intensities and stray directions are at
least partly attributable to lightning effects which become largely removed at
low field AF-demagnetization. Continued thermal demagnetization resulted
in breakdown of either an A- or a B-component. There was a slight prefer-
ence noticeable for the B-component to reside in the magnetic fraction with
the haematite-like blocking temperature range, and for the A-component to
reside in the magnetite-like fraction. In general, however, the Illara Sand-

### page_63
311
stone specimens conformed to the trend observed throughout this series of
studies, of a distinctive behaviour during thermal demagnetization. The
susceptibility decreased sharply above 450°C (Fig. 111.8). Only in some
specimens an AS0 component could be identified (Fig. 111.5).
Deception Formation. A normal and reversed polarity RFC constituting
20-80% of the initial intensity and prominent throughout the whole
sampled section, was broken down completely between 300°C and 500°C.
Pilot demagnetization studies revealed a blocking temperature range between
630” C and 670” C with a less evident range between 500” C and 570” C (Fig.
111.7). Some specimens displayed a disperse blocking temperature range
between 450” C and 670” C. A normal and reversed polarity AS0 component,
present throughout the section, became generally broken down between
400°C and 570°C and resided apparently in a magnetite phase. In some
specimens, however, the reversed polarity AS0 component became broken
down only at higher temperatures up to 675°C. A- and B-component direc-
tions of both normal and reversed polarity were equally well present
throughout the section. Notable was the occasional occurrence of both a
normal and a reversed B-component in the same specimen. More common
was the simultaneous occurrence of normal and reversed polarity B- and to a
lesser extent A-component directions in various specimens from the same
sample (Fig. 111.5). It was not possible to correlate the A- or the B-com-
ponent with a particular temperature interval in the range 400-67O”C.
Specimens with a dual polarity B-component invariably showed a breakdown
of the reversed component between 400°C and 580°C and of the normal
component between 580°C and 675°C. Throughout the lower sandy part of
the section, susceptibility remained fairly constant upon repeated heatings,
but the specimens from the upper more shaly part showed a susceptibility
decrease above 300°C (Fig. 111.8).
(B) Ross River section
Giles Creek Dolomite. The magnetic intensity in specimens from the
upper massive member was generally an order of magnitude lower than
in specimens from the lower mottled member, and was near the accuracy
limit of our cryogenic magnetometer. Application of orthogonal projection
figures, however, facilitated directional analysis of these specimens. An RFC,
constituting 40-60% of the initial intensity in samples from the lower
mottled sequence and up to 80% in samples from the upper massive
sequence, is evidently present in the NRM directions (Fig. 111.4.1). This
RFC component is generally completely broken down at 200°C (Figs. 111.5,
7). An AS0 component of reversed polarity is dominant throughout the
whole Giles Creek Dolomite section. In most samples of the lower part of
the section, this AS0 component was the only component which could be
identified in the temperature range 180-36O”C, with no other components
identifiable at higher temperatures. The primary magnetic component (A)

### page_64
312
was dominantly of reversed polarity, except for a probable interval of mixed
polarity at the base of the Giles Creek Dolomite and another well docu-
mented mixed polarity interval in the middle of the massive dolomitic
limestone member (Fig. 111.9A). In contrast, the B-component showed a
more frequent alternation of normal, reversed and mixed polarity intervals.
Breakdown of the A- and the B-component was gradual with no indication
whatsoever for a discrete blocking temperature range (Fig. 111.7). Samples
from the lower mottled member of the Giles Creek Dolomite show a very
rapid increase in susceptibility above 400” C (Fig, 111.8). In contrast, samples
from the upper massive member reveal a gradual susceptibility decrease
until1 300°C followed by an increase at higher temperatures.
Shannon Formation. Magnetic characteristics of the Shannon Formation
were rather similar to those from the Giles Creek Dolomite. An RFC of up
to 80% of the initial intensity (up to 95% in the uppermost site ASHK)
dominates the NRM directions (Fig. 111.4.1) and is broken down completely
at 200°C Figs. 111.5, 7). An AS0 component of reversed polarity which is
present throughout the formation, is eliminated in the temperature interval
200-320°C. Most of the specimens contain either an A-component or more
often a B-component which is broken down between 300°C and 450” C. In
the basal sites, the B-component is present with both normal and reversed
polarity directions, whereas the few B-component directions identified
higher up in the formation are of normal polarity only. A distinct reversal
pattern is present in the directions of the primary component. Reversed
polarity directions occur only in the basal sites, whereas the upper half of the
Pig. III.10. Equal area projection plots of formation mean direction. Squares = Areyonga
section, circles = Ross River Section. A. Primary magnetization component. B. “Cambro-
Ordovician” component. C. Recent field component (open symbols) and “Alice Springs
Orogeny” component (fuil symbols). Hexagon (D) = virtual direction at the sampling
locality according to the axial geocentric dipole model; inverted triangle (P) = present
local field direction at the sampling locality.

### page_65
313
formation reveals normal polarity directions only (Fig. III.SA). The declina-
tion of this E-W directed primary A-component of early-Late Cambrian
age is markedly different from the NW-SE declinations of the A-component
found in older formations of Middle Cambrian age in the Amadeus Basin and
in the Adelaide “Geosyncline” (Fig. IILSA, 10A). Similarly to the Giles
Creek Dolomite, all characteristic magnetic components became gradually
broken down, and no discrete blocking temperature range could be identi-
fied (Fig. 111.7). Susceptibility remained fairly constant throughout the
thermal treatment except for sites ASHH-ASH1 (stratigraphically high in
the formation) which showed a very rapid increase in susceptibility after
treatment above 400” C (Fig. 111.8).
INTERPRETATION
Clearly, separation and identification of the four magnetic components
present in the specimens would have been impossible without the applica-
tion of orthogonal projection figures (Zijderveld, 1967, 1975). A limiting
factor in the interpretation was the individual behaviour of the specimens
upon thermal demagnetization. No overall magnetic characteristics, other
than the appreciable difference in mean directions, were discernible to
separate the primary magnetic component (A) from the secondary magnetic
component (B). The spread in specimen directions attributed to either of
both groupings is fairly large and both distributions do in fact overlap.
Similar observations were made also in the accompanying studies on Cam-
brian sequences from the Adelaide “Geosyncline” (Sections I and II) to
which is referred for a more detailed discussion. By analogy to these studies
all specimen directions were subjected to a frequency analysis, the most
prominent directions were identified, and individual specimen directions
were attributed to one or the other of these groupings on the basis of their
proximity.
Four magnetic components, i.e., a recent field component (RFC) and
three characteristic components (ASO, Band A) have been identified through-
out both the red-bed sequence at Areyonga Gorge and the carbonate
sequence at Ross River (Figs. III.SA,B,lOA).
(A) Recent Field component (RFC)
In the Areyonga section this RFC is present as a normal polarity direction
only. This direction is intermediate between the present local field direction
and the expected local field direction according to the geocentric axial
dipole field model (Table 111.1, Figs. III.lOC, ll), and is thus most probably
of a recent origin. In the Ross River section, in contrast, both normal and
reversed polarity RFC directions are present (Fig. 111.11). Again the normal
polarity direction can be interpreted as being of recent origin (Figs. III.lOC,
11, Table 111.1). The few reversed polarity directions, however, show a
steeper than expected inclination.

### page_66

various recent field component directions obtained in the present studies from the
Adelaide “Geosyncline” (Sections I and II) and the Amadeus Basin The Mesozoic
(Schmidt, 1976) and Cenozoic (McElhinny et al., 1974a) part of the apparent polar
wander path for Australia (dots) is represented by the stages: 170-200 m.y., 100 m.y.,
40-60 my., 25-35 m.y., 20-25 m.y., 15-20 m.y., 5-10 my,, present. The inverted
triangles represent secondary magnetization components obtained by Schmidt et al.
(1976) and Luck (1970), attributed by Schmidt to a mid-Tertiary period of exten-
sive remagnetization. Diamonds represent a Maastrichtian-Early Eocene and
another Late Ohgocene pole position recently obtained by Idnurm and Senior (1978).

### page_67
315
Schmidt (1976) and Schmidt et al. (1976) report observations of second-
ary magnetic components, mostly of reversed polarity and of an obviously
fairly recent origin, in sediments from the Perth Basin (W. Australia), from
the Springfield Basin and from Kangaroo Island (Adelaide “Geosyncline”,
S. Australia) and quotes fairly similar observations for some Northern
Territory Formations as reported by Luck (1970).
Comparison of corresponding pole positions, with the Tertiary apparent
polar wander path for Australia (Wellman et al., 1969; McElhinny et al.,
1974a) led Schmidt to the interpretation, well established by his reversed
porality data, that these secondary magnetic components reflect a dominant
phase of lateritic weathering in Late Oligocene-Early Miocene times
(Woolnough, 1927), which incurred a synchronous remagnetization event
over a large part of Australia. The reversed polarity RFC directions (Fig.
111.1) obtained in the present Amadeus Basin study can be interpreted
in support of Schmidt’s hypothesis, but most of the RFC directions of both
normal and reversed polarity (Section II) observed in this series of studies
(I, II, III) are evidently - or may be interpreted in terms - of a more recent
origin. The “virtual” pole position corresponding with the present local field
direction at the sampling areas (Fig. III.ll), coincides with the Oligocene-
Miocene pole for Australia as obtained by McElhinny et al. (1974a). So,
obviously the streaking in RFC pole positions as shown in Fig. III.11 (2-13)
may equally well represent a sequence of remagnetization events spanning
the later half of the Cainozoic, as well as reflecting a remagnetization of very
recent origin, whose directions streak between the present local field direc-
tion at the sampling locality and the virtual direction expected according
to the geocentric axial dipole field model.
(B) Alice Springs Orogeny component (ASO)
This component is most dominantly present in the Ross River section,
where it occurs almost exclusively with a reversed polarity (Fig. III.SA),
but is less dominant in the Areyonga section, where both normal and
reversed polarity directions occur (Fig. III.SB). The pole position (Figs.
III.lBA, 13) corresponding to this ASO-component, after bedding correction
has been applied (Tables 111.1, 2, 3; Fig. III.lOC), fits nicely on the Devono-
Carboniferous segment of the mean polar wander path for Gondwanaland.
Therefore, this ASO-component can be well attributed to thermochemical
activity associated with the Alice Springs Orogeny which climaxed in the
Early Carboniferous (Wells, 1976). At least moderate reheating occurred
during this orogeny. This is clear from resetting of isotopic mineral ages in
the Arunta Complex, to the north and northeast of Ross River, Its
proximity to the more intensely affected areas may well explain the greater
dominancy of the AS0 component in the Ross River section than in the
Areyonga section.
The much improved grouping of the AS0 component directions when a

for samples from the Ellery Creek section and from the northeastern part of
the Amadeus Basin. Kirschvink also interpreted this ASO-component to be
of pretectonic origin. In contrast, McWilliams suggested a syn- to post-
tectonic origin. The reason for this discrepancy is not well understood. A
geographical differentiation in the timing of the main folding phase, as
suggested by J.L. Kirschvink (personal communication, 1978) possibly may
explain this observed disparity in results.
(C) The secondary B-component
This component of both normal and reversed polarity is very evident in
the Areyonga section, but less so in the Ross River section (Figs. III.4C, 9,
10, Tables 111.1, 2). Comparison with the main Gondwanaland APW (Figs.
111.12, 13) indicates that this component was acquired prior to the Alice
Springs Orogeny. However, apart from some middle Palaeozoic periods of
minor tectonic instability in the Amadeus Basin, i.e. the Rodingan Move-
ment and the Perntjara Movement, and the Bloodwood Movement in the
adjacent Ngalia Basin, the latter not better defined than the period early-
Middle Cambrian to Late Ordovician (A.T. Wells, personal communication,
1978), there is nothing in the tectonic record which could be associated with
acquisition of this component. The pole positions corresponding with this

### page_72
320
component are in remarkably good agreement with those from a similar
secondary magnetic component noted in the Adelaide “Geosyncline” (Figs.
111.9, 12A, B). Both in the Flinders Ranges (Section I) and in the Kangaroo
Island (Section II) studies, acuisition of this secondary magnetic component
was attributed to thermo-chemical activity associated with a phase of
regional heating which predated the main folding phases of the Late Cam-
brian-Early Ordovician Delamarian Orogeny. Although not noted in the
Amadeus Basin, Williams (1975) suggested that metamorphic effects of this
orogeny extend far to the north of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” into the
Pedirka Basin. Therefore, acquisition of this B-component due to thermo-
chemical activity during a period of similarly enhanced heat flux may be
envisaged for the Amadeus Basin also. The blanketing effect of the later
Alice Springs Orogeny may well have obscured any traces from such a Late
Cambrian-Ordovician heating in the Amadeus Basin. The presence of both
normal and reversed polarities of this secondary component points to a
prolonged thermo-chemical activity.
Such an acquisition mechanism for this B-component seems the more
likely as a strongly increased heat flux during Late Cambrian-Early Ordo-
vician times characterizes the Pan-African erogenic belts of Gondwanaland
(Krylov, 1972). During this period, widespread isotopic resetting occurred in
such zones as the Damaran-Katangan belt in Africa (Clifford, 1970), along
the Pacific border of Gondwanaland (Craddock, 1977) and in particular the
Transantarctic Mountains (Veevers, 1976), along the Indian East Coast
(Crawford, 1969) and along the Proto-Atlantic margin (Hurley et al., 1968;
Hurley, 1972).
(0) The primary A-component
The mere fact that this primary magnetic component could be separated
and determined despite three subsequent and dominant phases of magnetic
overprinting may serve as an illustration of the resolution power of ortho-
gonal projection figures (Zijderveld, 1967, 1975) in magnetically complex
systems. In the Middle Cambrian Areyonga section (Tempe Formation,
Illara Sandstone, Deception Formation) this A-component shows a very
rapid alternation and intermixing of normal and reversed polarities (Fig.
III.SB). Occasionally both polarities are present in various specimens from
the same sample. This persistent dual polarity behaviour of the A-component
in the Areyonga red-bed sequence contrasts sharply with the correlatable
Middle Cambrian carbonate sequence from the Ross River sequence (Fig.
IILSA). Throughout the Giles Creek Dolomite, reversed polarities seem to
dominate completely. Sole exceptions are a section of mixed polarity in the
middle of the massive upper member, and possibly a less well established
mixed polarity sequence in the lower member (Fig. III.SA). Correlation of
the whole dual polarity Areyonga section with either of these short mixed
polarity intervals in the Giles Creek Dolomite seems a remote solution for

### page_73
321
this discrepancy in polarity structure between both sections. It seems more
likely that the dual polarity structure of the Areyonga red-bed sequence is
due to a prolonged acquisition of magnetization upon diagenesis, lasting for
at least a normal and a reversed polarity event. Similar observations (Fig.
111.15) were noted also for red-bed sequences from the Flinders Ranges
(Section I) and from Kangaroo Island (Section II). In the carbonate
sequences studied here, however, such a dual polarity structure was notably
absent or of very minor prominence. This may point to a shorter acquisition
phase for the primary magnetization in case of such carbonate sediments. It
is open to verification whether the difference observed here in polarity
structure between the red beds and carbonate rocks, represents a more
general occurrence. Clearly, application of the red bed results reported here
for magnetostratigraphic purposes is subject to serious limitation.
The Middle Cambrian directions from the Amadeus Basin (Tempe Forma-
tion, Illara Sandstone, Deception Formation, Giles Creek Dolomite), agree
well amongst themselves. This supports the suggested Middle Cambrian age
of the Illara Sandstone and the Deception Formation (Wells et al., 1970),
which was based on the superposition principle only. However, they clearly
differ from the early-Late Cambrian results from the Shannon Formation.
These Middle Cambrian results from the Amadeus Basin are also consistent
with results from correlatable formations from the Adelaide “Geosyncline”
(Figs. IILlBB, 13), and imply a much reduced polar motion for the Middle
Cambrian. Rapid polar motion began again in the late-Early Cambrian as is
evidenced by the results from the Shannon Formation (Fig. 111.14). Like
the underlying Giles Creek Dolomite, this Shannon Formation (early-Late
Cambrian) shows a well defined polarity pattern. The reversed polarity zone
in the top part of the Giles Creek Dolomite continues into the basal part of
the Shannon Formation, followed by a normal polarity sequence in its
upper half (Figs. III.SA, 15). The declination record (Fig. III.lOA) shows a
swing from SW-NE pointing declinations in the Middle Cambrian to E-W
pointing declinations in the early-Late Cambrian. Rapid polar movement
probably continued during the Cambro-Ordovician as indicated by the
sequence of pole positions from the B-component (Figs. III.lBA, 14).
The latest Proterozoic-early Palaeozoic interval is thus characterized by
periods of much reduced polar movement (quasi static intervals) alternating
with periods of rapid polar movement (Figs. 111.14, 15). Concentric direc-
tions obtained by Kirschvink (1978b) from formations spanning the Pre-
cambrian--Cambrian boundary (Pertatataka Formation, Arumbera Sandstone
s.l., Eninta Formation and the Todd River Dolomite) led him to the sugges-
tion of a quasi static interval for this period. The alternative explanation of
magnetic resetting due to the Petermann Ranges Orogeny (600 m.y.) seems
somewhat unlikely as its effects are mostly localized to the southwestern
margin of the Amadeus Basin, whereas Kirschvink sampled in the north-
eastern part. Early Cambrian data from the Hawker Group of the Flinders
Ranges (Section I) may suggest rapid polar movement, although an alter-

IMPLICATIONS
Despite obvious problems in interpreting the polarity structure of arenitic
red-bed sequences in both the Adelaide “Geosyncline” (Sections I and II)

### page_75
FLINOERS RS. AMADEUS BASIN -US W M.AYERlCA
I(ANGAA00 ISL. AREYONGA GGSS RNI lnw wNALSTGElG7G
s
_i I
Fig. 111.15. Magnetostratigraphic correlation of the late Proterozoic-Cambrian forma-
tions from the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and the Amadeus Basin, compared with a ten-
tative polarity zonation for western North America.
and in the Amadeus Basin, a general polarity pattern for the Cambrian of
Australia can be constructed (Fig. 111.15). This shows a predominance of
reversed polarities throughout the Early, Middle and earliest-Late Cambrian
with some periods of mixed polarity intercalated, which are partly of doubt-
ful nature as pointed out before (earliest Cambrian: Todd River Dolomite
(Kirschvink, 1978a, b), Parachilna Formation; Ajax Limestone; late-Early
Cambrian: Billy Creek Formation?; Kangaroo Island sequence?; early-Middle
Cambrian: Aroona Creek Limestone, Wirrealpa Limestone; late-Middle
Cambrian: Giles Creek Dolomite). This longlasting phase of reversed polarity
is followed by a period of normal polarity starting in the early-Late Cam-
brian, shortly preceded by inception of a continuing rapid polar movement
(Shannon Formation). Clearly, similar trends are also visible in the pre-
dominantly reversed polarity pattern of early Palaeozoic sequences from
western North America (Fig. 15; D. van Alstine, personal communication,
1978). Although some discrepancies in timing may have to be updated, both

### page_76
324
the Australian and the North American pattern may well serve as a basis for
intercontinental correlation.
The good agreement between both the primary Middle Cambrian and the
secondary Cambro-Ordovician results from the Amadeus Basin and from the
Adelaide “Geosyncline” refute Harrington et al’s (1973) hypothesis for
substantial rifting in the Australian Plate during Middle and Late Cambrian
times. An earlier, latest Proterozoic inition of the rifting as suggested by
Harrington et al. (1973) cannot be ruled out, as a discrepancy in pole posi-
tions exists indeed between the Early Cambrian Todd River Dolomite results
(Kirschvink, 1978b) from the Amadeus Basin and the cursory results from
the Early Cambrian Hawker Group of the Flinders Ranges (Section I). It
seems more likely, however, that the results represent various trajectories
of the APW during a period of rapid polar wandering. This interpretation
contrasts with McWilliams’ (1977) analysis of newly obtained late Protero-
zoic palaeomagnetic results from Australia, which he interpreted in support
of Harrington et al.% (1973) model.
Clearly the early Palaeozoic part of the common apparent polar wander
path for Gondwanaland as proposed by McElhinny et al. (1974b; McElhinny
and Embleton, 1976) has to be updated considerably on the basis of new
palaeomagnetic results from the early Palaeozoic of Australia as detailed in
this series of studies (Sections I, II and III). The early Palaeozoic part of the
originally proposed APW path was not completely satisfactorily defined as
several pole positions, notably from the Adelaide “Geosyncline”, appeared
to be out of sequence, whilst some South American and African data did
not conform to this path at all. This latter group of results is now supported,
however, by the Cambro-Ordovician pole positions for Australia obtained
here, and some of McWilliams (1977) results from late Proterozoic rocks
from Southern Africa and from widely different areas in Australia can be
interpreted in further support.
Palaeomagnetic studies on early Palaeozoic and older rocks face problems
of (1) separation of individual components in a multicomponent magnetic
system, (2) identification of the various components as primary and second-
ary magnetizations, (3) the ambiguity in polarity assignment. McWilliams’
(1977) study is a fine example of separation of magnetic components
through analytical and graphical (orthogonal projections) analysis of a multi-
component magnetization system. McWilliams found secondary magnetic
components which adhere rather well to the presently found secondary
B-components of Cambro-Ordovician age (Fig. 111.13), in data from
Southern Africa (Nosib Group-Blaubeker Formation - NBF, Nosib Group -
NGR), and from Australia (Egan Tillite (Kimberley Basin) - ETS, Chambers
Bluff Volcanics (Officer Basin) - CBVSl, the Wooltana Volcanics - WVS
and the Merinjina Tillite - MTS, in the Northern Flinders Ranges). More-
over, after reversing of his polarity interpretation comparable results from
the Chuas-Maieberg Formation (CMF) and the Lower Nama Group (LNG)
from Southern Africa may be better interpreted in terms of a secondary

### page_77
325
Cambro-Ordovician magnetization than in terms of a primary magnetization
as originally suggested by McWilliams. McWilliams’ (1977) results from the
King Island Volcanics (KIV) and the King Island dykes (KID) also fit rather
well with this pattern. These formations are of an unspecified but probably
early Palaeozoic age, so such a Cambro-Ordovician magnetic component may
equally well represent either a primary or a secondary magnetization.
An updated version of the common APW for Gondwanaland as originally
proposed by McElhinny et al. (1974b; McElhinny and Embleton, 1976) is
presented in Fig. III.l3A, B. The most significant change has been made to
the early Palaeozoic part of the APW (Fig. 111.13A) with the addition of the
Cambro-Ordovician loop. The suggested halfloops in the Cambrian part of
the APW are open to refinement. In the absence of better data, some of the
earlier Australian results had to be included, in which possibly an equally
present overprinting has not yet been identified. The younger part of the
common APW (late Palaeozoic-Middle Jurassic) remained largely un-
changed. The pole positions for the detailed Devono-Carboniferous AS0
component show good agreement with the path (Fig. 13B).
McElhinny et al. (1974b; McElhinny and Embleton, 1976) suggested
backwards continuation of the common APW till at least 750 m.y. ago,
which infers a long standing unity of Gondwanaland. An alternative solution
was recently proposed by McWilliams (1977) who noted that pole positions
from the various Gondwana continents appear to be concentrated mainly
in different parts of the late Proterozoic loop. The African data are promi-
nent in the “early” part, whereas the Australian data dominate the “later”
half. This led McWilliams to an alternative solution of separate APW’s for
eastern (Australia, Antarctica and India) and western Gondwanaland (Africa,
South America), which join each other in the Early Cambrian trajectory.
Thus inferring a collision origin for at least part of the Pan-African erogenic
belts. McWilliams’ (1977) suggestion was based quite substantially on a
reconfiguration of Australian pole positions according to the Cambrian frag-
mentation model (Harrington et al., 1973), which is not substantiated by the
Middle Cambrian data presented here (Sections I-III). Moreover, the
Cambro-Ordovician loop proposed here in the Gondwanaland APW facilitates
alternative interpretations for the polarity and also for a secondary rather
than a primary nature of the magnetization of various earlier palaeomag-
netic results. Admittedly, a wide range of APW paths can be constructed
through the palaeomagnetically ill defined late Proterozoic interval, and the
here advanced combined Gondwanaland APW (Fig. 111.13) is only proposed
as one of the many possible trajectories. It is, however, a natural consequence
of the model, based as it is on the present findings of thermo-chemically
induced secondary magnetic components of Cambro-Ordovician age in vari-
ous areas of Australia and possible beyond, notably observed in absence of
contemporaneous deformation, and the widespread evidence for an enhanced
heat flux in the Pan-African erogenic belts during Cambro-Ordovician times,
that it suggests an ensialic rather than a collision origin as the more favour-
able model for the Pan-African belts in Gondwanaland.

### page_78
326
CONCLUSIONS
Four magnetic components have been identified in a red-bed sequence
from the Areyonga Gorge (central Amadeus Basin) and in a carbonate
sequence from the Ross River Gorge (eastern Amadeus Basin).
(A) A recent component (RFC) of both normal and reversed polarity. In
some of the fo~ations studied, this RFC is clearly of latest Cainozoic
origin, but an earlier acquisition, possibly related to a widespread middle
Tertiary laterization event, cannot be excluded for other formations.
(B) A Late Devonian-Early Carboniferous component (ASO) induced
prior to the main folding phase of the Alice Springs Orogeny (Early Carbonif-
erous). This component is most domin~tly present in the Ross River Gorge
(nearly exclusively reversed polarities} and to a lesser extent in the Areyonga
Gorge (reversed and normal polarities).
(C) A secondary component (B) of both normal and reversed polarity,
which is very similar to a Late Cambrian-Early Ordovician secondary com-
ponent which became induced in rocks from the Adelaide “Geosyncline” by
enhanced the~o~hemic~ activity during a period of enhanced heat flux
prior to the Delamarian Orogeny. In absence of indications for early Palaeo-
zoic tectonic activity in the Amadeus Basin, a similar thermo-chemical
acquisition is envisaged also for this B component.
(D) A primary magnetic component (A). Middle Cambrian directions from
both the Areyonga section and the Ross River sequence group very well,
whereas early-Late Camb~an directions from the Shannon Formation (Ross
River) indicate onset of appreciably polar wandering.
The present data compared with Kirschvink’s (1978b) Precambrian-
Cambrian boundary period results from several Amadeus Basin sequences
group into two quasi static intervals spanning the Precambrian-Cambrian
boundary period and the Middle Cambrian, which alternate with periods of
rather fast polar movement during the Early Cambrian and the Cambro-
Ordovician.
Thermal demagnization study on red-bed sequences and carbonate
sequences in the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the Amadeus Basin indicate
that the former are generally less suited for magnetostratigraphic applica-
tions, as acquisition of their “primary” magnetization probably took place
over a prolonged period. In contrast, the red-bed sequences generally showed
a better concentration of component directions when compared with the
carbonate sequences.
The combined data from the Amadeus Basin and the Adelaide “Geosyn-
cline ” indicate the Early- and Middle Cambrian as a dominantly reversed
polarity interval with some periods of mixed polarity intercalated. A normal
polarity interval seems to have started in the early-Late Cambrian. This
pattern compares well with a preliminary early Palaeozoic polarity strati-
graphy for North America.
Magnetic components similar to the thermo-chemically induced Cambro-

### page_79
327
Ordovician components in the Amadeus Basin, and in the Adelaide “Geo-
syncline” were reported recently from widely different areas in Australia and
in Southern Africa by McWilliams (1977), who also suggested as secondary
early Palaeozoic origin for most of them. It is quite possible that this set of
secondary magnetizations results from an enhanced thermo-chemical activity
during Cambro-Ordovician times, associated with formation of Pan-African
Orogenic belts of Gondwanaland.
The good agreement between Middle Cambrian poles from the Amadeus
Basin and from the Adelaide “Geosyncline” refutes Harrington et al.%
(1973) hypothesis of fragmentation of the Australian plate during Middle
and Late Cambrian times. A possible earlier fragmentation cannot be ruled
out, however, on grounds of the present data.
An earlier proposed common APW for Gondwanaland (McElhinny et al.,
1974b; McElhinny and Embleton, 1976) has been updated. Unity of Gond-
wanaland backwards till at least 750 m.y. ago seems well in accord with
existing evidence, but alternative interpretations (McWilliams, 1977) remain
equally possible.
